subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS BY TJ.S. RESPECTING DIVERSION FROM HUDSON BAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister in his capacity as Secretary of State for External Affairs, and ask him whether representations have been made to Canada by the United States state department in connection with the water levels of the great lakes, and with particular reference to a diversion out of the Hudson bay watershed to the great lakes. If that is so, could the Prime Minister tell us the nature of the representations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS BY TJ.S. RESPECTING DIVERSION FROM HUDSON BAY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman gave me notice of this question a few moments ago, and I have endeavoured to secure the latest information. As of yesterday no representations had been received on this matter from the state department. I should add that from time to time various proposals have been made for a diversion of water from the Hudson bay watershed to permit an additional diversion at Chicago, but as far as this government is concerned it stands unalterably opposed to any further diversion of water at the request of Chicago.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in that part of the blue book of estimates entitled "Transport" there are several dozen votes, together with three or four items authorized by statute, pertaining to the Department of Transport and several other government agencies which report to parliament. A quick glance at the bottom of page 82 will show that these appropriations total $287,468,802.
The first allotment to which I will direct the attention of the committee is vote 404, aids to navigation, construction, to be found on page 75. This vote is up by approximately 70 per cent. A large expenditure is associated with construction of our new marine agency depot at Charlottetown. This project, begun in 1958, requires several years for completion. The Department of Public Works administers this type of construction for us; and we are providing $500,000 for wharf construction.
Another work of a similar type will be completed this year at Saint John, New Brunswick. There we must spend $250,000 to wind up construction of the agency complex which we began four years ago. We will also embark on a wharf extension project at Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. The $200,000 which the Department of Public Works expects to spend on our behalf represents the first portion of an outlay of some $2,200,000.
Erection of lighthouse piers will be pushed ahead in line with our program for installation of the most modern aids for the assistance of shipping. One of these items alone, the light station at Prince shoal in the St. Lawrence river, represents the largest single outlay in the appropriation, namely $700,000. Eacilities at our Quebec city agency will be improved at a cost of $250,000.
There is another proposal related to the trend toward modernization. Many of our light stations are isolated, and the attendants and their families are cut off from contact with other people. When weather conditions are particularly bad the delivery of supplies or the evacuation of sick persons cannot be performed. With a view to lessening the hardships on these employees we propose to construct helicopter landing platforms at several
Supply-Transport
stations this year. If this experiment proves successful it will, of course, be extended to many other locations.
Increased shipping activity from the seaway is reflected in the decision to construct modern type establishments at Prescott, Ontario, to replace the structure destroyed by fire last year and other obsolete facilities. The overall cost of that work will be $1.5 million. Among the many other specific points at which major works will be performed are Victoria and Prince Rupert, British Columbia, and St. John's, Newfoundland.
Despite its very short existence, the St. Lawrence seaway has already resulted in a very definite-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I wonder if we could have a little more quiet in the committee so that those of us who want to follow what the minister is saying can do so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I agree with the hon. member. I think private conversation should be continued in a much quieter tone.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
This very definite trend about which I was speaking is borne out quite conclusively by an examination of the annual reports of the seaway authority and the national harbours board. Both agencies have reported the movement and handling of more cargo by fewer but larger ships. Quite clearly this emphasizes the urgency of maintaining and improving shipping channels in the St. Lawrence and Saguenay rivers. With this in mind we are planning to construct and operate, at a cost of some $350,000, a hydraulic model of the river section below Montreal.
The long term capital dredging program, begun five years ago, for widening critical sections and deepening other areas in the ship channel will be advanced considerably with the expenditure of some $3| million.
The summarized detail in the estimates book discloses that total moneys proposed with respect to our marine services aggregate something over $63 million. That figure represents an increase of 24 per cent over the related total for 1960-61. I think I should, therefore, explain the reason for this.
The recommended programs for aids to navigation and ship channel work, to which I have already referred, account for about $4 million of the increase. The largest single appropriation is that operation and maintenance of the Canadian marine service, our departmental fleet. Here we will be holding to an outlay almost identical with last year's appropriation. The $18.8 million we have allotted pertains to expenditures associated with design of new vessels, as well as refit,

Supply-Transport
conversion, repairs and operation of our fleet of icebreakers, supply and buoy vessels, weather ships and northern service vessels.
Next in order of size is the vote for construction or acquisition, for which $15.5 million is provided. This vote shows the largest increase percentagewise of our 40-odd departmental appropriations. During the past year our ship construction program levelled off very appreciably. We were then witnessing completion of numerous large units. Apart from this, our ship construction organization was engaged in the preparation of plans and specifications for additional ships. That planning has now progressed to the point where we are able to embark on actual construction. To illustrate this aspect of the proposed program set out in this appropriation, let me point out that approximately $11 million is labeled for additional vessels.
I shall give a rundown on the larger projects. There is first a triple screw icebreaker, similar in type to the John A. Macdonald which entered service last year. It is hoped to commence construction some time this fall, with completion billed for the fall of 1964. Included in the proposed new starts is one unit which will differ somewhat in type and function from any of our existing vessels. I am sure all members of this committee are aware of the publicity given to breaks occurring in trans-Atlantic cables fanning out from our shores. This has been a matter of some concern to the government, for the loss of revenue resulting from so much as one day's interruption in service is very appreciable. In addition, it is a fact that there is a very decided shortage of cable repair ships, and this country must depend on other nations for assistance. It is proposed, therefore, to construct a dual type unit suitable for cable repair work and for icebreaking. When not engaged on the former work, this ship will be used on normal departmental tasks. The total cost may go as high as $7.5 million, and we have included approximately $2 million for the initial construction work.
For the past 10 years the department has operated, under international agreement, two weather ships in the Pacific ocean. After careful consideration extending over the past couple of years, it has been decided we should take action to replace the two ships. This decision is based on two factors. The ships are wartime frigates of the R.C.N. converted for this particular assignment, and maintenance costs have become excessive. Furthermore, a broadened demand for scientific data tends to make the ships quite unsuitable. The two new ships will cost some $8 million each. The department is now conferring with other departments to determine suitability
[Mr. Balcer.l
of design. This is not an easy matter to resolve, because the ships must serve such diversified requirements as meteorology, oceanography, hydrography, search and rescue, aircraft guidance, etc. Subject to settlement of the design feature, we plan on getting construction under way in the latter part of this year.
During the past few years my predecessor in office has kept hon. members informed of the very heavy work load we have assumed regarding transportation of cargo to the far north in support of domestic and international activities, both civil and military. Each succeeding year our techniques are being improved upon, so much so that the hazardous assignment of a few years ago has become somewhat routine today. Despite this transition, however, the operation continues to be one which imposes rigorous working conditions for our personnel. It is for this reason that we have included in our program an item of $1.5 million for a depot ship which will provide living accommodation for stevedores.
I am sure that representatives of east and west coast areas will be specially interested in another part of our shipbuilding program. Announcement was made in 1960 of the government's intention to improve our marine search and rescue operations as well as safety practices among shipping operators. In line with that decision we intend to provide, at a cost of some $4 million, eight high speed cutters-five large and three small-which will operate on both coasts and in the great lakes. Barring any unforeseen delay we should have these cutters ready in the summer or autumn of 1962.
The 1961-62 vote bearing No. 413 should be explained inasmuch as it appears to be approximately five times the last appropriation. Actually this vote is a consolidation of two or three appropriations appearing separately in past years. This has resulted from a reorganization of the establishment which links together pilotage, steamship inspection and marine reporting service. Apart from that, a few large construction projects are contemplated. Present temporary accommodation for the pilotage station at Les Escoumains, Quebec, will be replaced by a new station at Anse aux Basques, at a cost of $750,000. The Department of Public Works will construct for us at Clarenville, Newfoundland, a marine haul-out and a fitting-out wharf. Vote 413 contains $400,000 for these facilities, which will permit the inspection and repair of ships of up to 500 tons capacity. Another proposal related to improvement of the pilotage service rendered to shipping involves an expenditure of some $900,000 to replace obsolete pilot boats at Sydney, Halifax, Saint John, New Brunswick, and Vancouver.

Grouped together in the blue book under the heading "Railway and Steamship Services" there are 12 votes totalling $32 million plus, a slight increase over last year's figure. I shall comment very briefly on the larger of the individual changes. Moneys required for the auto-ferry vessel for the Prince Edward Island car ferry service are considerably less; the ship will be completed in the latter part of this year. The item for improvements to the terminal at North Sydney is likewise decreased by approximately $400,000, and for the same reason. The project related to additional railway trackage undertaken last summer is now finished.
We find it necessary to increase by $1,175,000 the allowance for the anticipated deficit in operation of the Newfoundland ferry services and terminals. The Canadian National Railways, who operate the service on behalf of the government, anticipate a slight increase in revenue, but operating expenses are expected to be a good deal higher.
The blue book comparison also indicates a sizeable increment in the deficit for the Prince Edward Island ferry service. The increase shown is $546,000. This is to a certain extent misleading, because subsequent to the preparation of these estimates a final supplementary vote increased the 1960-61 appropriation by $322,000. Thus the expected net increase for 1961-62 is $224,000.
Last year parliament approved an expenditure of $325,000 for improvements to the Cape Tormentine terminal of the Prince Edward Island ferry service. This work was necessary to permit efficient use of the vessels now operated. With the commissioning of the new ship to which I referred just now a total of four ships will be operating during the peak traffic season. Since this will overtax the facilities at Borden, it is proposed, therefore, to build a new ferry dock there at a cost of $980,000.
The lengthy, diversified list of services, programs, functions and responsibilities which are grouped together under the air services of my department accounts for some $155 million of the total funds we are asking parliament to provide. In relation to the main estimates for the last fiscal year, this proposed total outlay means an increase of some $15 million. This is, of course, indicative of the ever expanding requirements we must expect in our efforts to cope with the trend toward travel by air.
Just to demonstrate the tremendous growth in this area of public expenditure, let me point out that funds voted ten years ago, that is for 1951-52, amounted to $39 million. Other illustrations of this growth factor are easy to find in any study of this area. In the same decade the number of Canadian civil
Supply-Transport
aircraft licensed has multiplied; it was 1,960 aircraft at the end of 1950 and is now 5,400. Examination of personnel licensing records disclosed an almost identical rate of growth. We find that for each type of licensing there is a remarkably consistent increase of 15 per cent each year.
Let me mention here some significant detail on the traffic side of the picture. Whereas in 1950 our Canadian operators carried slightly more than 1 million passengers, in 1959 they transported close to 5 million. Carriage of goods showed a fourfold increase.
To compound the problems presented by this growing acceptance of air travel we now have the demands of the jet age. The noise level and greater space requirements are, in many instances, forcing design changes in airport construction. Runways have to be lengthened and strengthened, greater allowances are required for apron and hangar space and fuel storage. Location of airports in turn demands innovations to speed up refuelling, loading, unloading and shortening of taxiing distances; otherwise the advantage of speed will be lost. The more critical performance standards of jet aircraft demand other requirements as well. A good example is the more sophisticated traffic control services and the growing acceptance of some element of automation.
Proper administration of the numerous programs planned for the meteorological, telecommunications and civil aviation branches during the next year will most certainly make for a heavy work load, so much so that we must seek approval for a staff increase of 243 positions. This augmented staff will total 9,809 positions.
I do not intend to try to spell out in any great detail the many constituent parts of the various proposed activities. To do so I would be obliged to deal with a number of separate divisions, each of which in turn has a variety of activities, such as construction, operation, regulation, etc. I shall therefore attempt to single out particular items which I believe will be of greatest interest to the members of this committee.
The very large sum of $60,900,000 is set down for all types of construction related to airports, whether this be terminal buildings, runways, service buildings, taxiways, parking aprons, approach lighting, power plants, seaplane docks, water or sewage services. Within the last few years increasing emphasis has been given to the establishment of a series of modern air terminal buildings which will soon extend the length of our trans-Canada airway. In 1930 we saw that objective brought much closer with completion of our terminals at Montreal, Regina, Halifax and Ottawa. Very substantial progress likewise

Supply-Transport
was made on the structures at Edmonton, Winnipeg and Toronto. For these latter three projects alone the sum of $20.5 million is provided in these estimates. Numerous other points should witness air terminal building construction this year, for example North Bay, Sault Ste. Marie, Port Hardy, Victoria, Fort McMurray, and Prince Rupert and Penticton. Some of these are projects we had, in fact, planned to start last year, but changes in requirements and internal reallocations of funds have led us to institute revised planning.
A significant change appears in the two appropriations related to both the operation and the construction of radio aids for air and marine navigation, and again the change is upward. I refer to the two allotments on page 80 of the estimates book, which total some $33 million. The programs envisaged here do not lend themselves to ready explanation. One reason for this is the technical nature of the work. Then, too, the various systems of communication facilities are so dispersed that one cannot pinpoint expenditures by specific locations.
I would, however, like to apprise this committee of one particular assignment to be added to the work of this section of the department this year. This is the operation of four chains of DECCA navigator stations, a task heretofore performed for us by a commercial agency.

speechtext: What is the name of the stations?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the committee is grateful to the minister for the very comprehensive statement he has just given us, breaking down the various items of his department into a number of divisions which will enable us to consider these estimates with greater clarity than we otherwise could. 1 have some comments I should like to make regarding these divisions of his department, and I shall make them as I go along.
First, I should like to reiterate my congratulations to the minister on his appointment to what I have always considered the finest and best department in the government service. I have no hesitation in adding to that my best wishes to the minister for a happy but short tenure of office.
My first suggestion is one which may not meet with the approval of the minister but which I feel should commend itself to the consideration of a government that intends to deal with this huge department in an objective way. One has but to look at the estimates of the Department of Transport and consider the very wide field that the department covers to come to one conclusion; that it is extremely difficult for any one individual to administer the activities of a department of that size effectively and in the manner in which they should be administered. I am sure the minister will understand that I make that suggestion objectively without in any way wanting to be derogatory to himself. One has but to look at the annual report of the Department of Transport to appreciate what this department contains.
The department can be divided under three main headings: railway services, waterway services and air services, which in themselves are tremendous. But when one looks
Supply-Transport
at the many corporations and boards which are also responsible to the minister, such as Canadian National Railways, Trans-Canada Air Lines, Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation, the air transport board, the board of transport commissioners, the maritime commission, the St. Lawrence seaway, and many other such agencies for which the minister is responsible, one can appreciate how vast the department is.
To strengthen my argument, I suggest there should be added to the Department of Transport such other communication matters as the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which are assigned to one particular minister because of their importance. That was the policy of the former government, and it has been followed by this government. However, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and all its affiliations are matters which normally should come under the department having to do with transportation. That is why I suggest that the ministry of transport should be divided into two parts, one having to do with air services, under which would come civil aviation, meteorological services and communication services, together with the crown corporations, boards and commissions that normally fall under those three headings. Under the jurisdiction of the other part could come other services that fall under the Department of Transport such as rail services and waterway services, together with the crown corporations, agencies, commissions and boards relating to those services. It seems to me, sir, that this is not an illogical division. Because of the tremendous importance which this department takes on year in and year out, the government should give consideration to this suggestion.
I move to another point which has to do with the railways. What is the position of the Canadian railways? It had a huge deficit in 1960; I think the amount was $65 million or $70 million. A large deficit for 1961 has also been prophesied. A threatened strike has just been averted by the operators of the railways and their employees. When one refers to that threatened strike one cannot do other than ask the government where it is going with reference to railway services in this country.
Some time ago the Prime Minister set up the MacPherson royal commission on transportation. It has brought down four recommendations involving subsidies of about $97 million. What is the policy of the government with reference to these four recommendations? We have asked repeatedly in this house for information in that respect and we have received none, save that the policy of the

Supply-Transport
government will be announced in due course. That is not what the Prime Minister said in November of last year when we were face to face with a railway strike. It is important for the people of Canada and the members of the House of Commons to know what is to be done with respect to those recommendations.
There is on the order paper now a bill having to do with the Freight Rates Reduction Act, with which we shall be dealing early next week. A statement has been made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport in that regard, and I shall not take up the time of the committee in commenting on it other than to say that on the one hand we have the board of transport commissioners, which cannot make freight rates retroactive; it cannot reduce freight rates retroactively. On the other hand we have the minister and the Prime Minister saying that the Freight Rates Reduction Act will be made retroactive. How these two things are going to be reconciled I do not know. Perhaps I should not put it positively, but rather should ask the question. How does an act of parliament giving a freight rate reduction retroactively jibe with the policy of the board of transport commissioners, which is based on the Railway Act, which clearly states that freight rates cannot be reduced or increased retroactively? These are matters that we shall be discussing during the course of next week.
I come back to the threatened strike which was settled recently, because I asked the very important question in the house, where was the money to come from? We all remember what the Prime Minister said when this matter was under discussion in November of last year. I should like to put on record what he said as reported at page 359 of Hansard of November 30, 1960:
It will make its report as to the means whereby these discriminatory rates may be avoided. Legislation will then be introduced in order to equalize opportunity across Canada. The freeze will then be taken off and the railway companies may then make an application to the board of transport commissioners to raise the freight rates and to take into consideration the agreements now in existence between the employers and the unions back to January 1, 1960.
Legislation will be introduced in parliament. First the Prime Minister said that the royal commission on transportation would bring in a formula that would settle the dispute. Well, if they brought in a formula it certainly did not settle the dispute. Then the Prime Minister said that legislation would follow. It is there in black and white. Notwithstanding our demands of the Prime Minister as to what was going to be done with the recommendations made by the royal commission, he said that the policy would

be announced in due course. There is no question of legislation, although the report was made some weeks ago.
The Prime Minister said that the freeze would be lifted and the railways would then be in a position to make an application to the board in order, I presume, to take into consideration the agreements in existence between the employers and the unions. Therefore I think I am justified in asking the question, where is the money to come from? Does the minister not think it is about time for the government to make known its policy on this whole matter of railway transporta^ tion in Canada, as was done yesterday with reference to shipping policy, about which I shall have something to say later on.
The point is that the railways find themselves in a difficult position, and I think it is the duty of the government to tell the country what its policy is to be, not only in the general field, having regard to the report of the MacPherson commission, but in the other field that I mentioned. I should like to put on Hansard what the Prime Minister said on May 10 in his television broadcast on "The Nation's Business":
I think most Canadians will welcome the fact that the railway strike scheduled to take place next week has been averted. Some opposition members, you should have seen them in the house, they were far from happy when it was announced. They looked disturbed.
This is not a statement which should come from the Prime Minister. I said in the house, and I repeat now, that all Canadians should have been pleased and I am sure were pleased that a railway strike was averted. This kind of statement comes with ill grace from the Prime Minister in so far as it is a reflection upon the members of the opposition. Then he went on to say:
The action we have taken and the stand we took last fall has been fully vindicated.
That is not so; that is a complete inaccuracy. I continue:
And yet what happened last fall? The members of the Liberal party and the C.C.F. party voted against the legislation, but the vocal critics of last December are not so noisy now in the month of May.
Well, just let us pause for a moment and see what happened. The dispute was settled on the very basis of the recommendation made by the Liberal party. The Liberal party suggested to the government that the dispute be settled on the basis of the majority report of the conciliation board, known as the Mil-vain report.

By
compulsory arbitration, you mean; that is what you suggested.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
And the Liberal opposition made it quite clear where it stood in so far as a strike was concerned. The conclusions that have been reached in the settlement of the strike are the same as those that were recommended from this side of the house. Therefore it ill becomes the Prime Minister to be blowing oft steam because of the fact that he or the government by inference have been responsible for the settlement of the strike.
I say to the minister that we were the ones who were in the right in reference to this matter. The government was wrong, because the agreement was not according to the procedure described by the Prime Minister. I have put on record the statement made by the Prime Minister as to the manner in which this matter would be dealt with, and there is no doubt that is not the way in which the strike was settled. It was done on an entirely different basis. According to the statement which I put on record, the railways were not supposed to receive any subsidy from the government but would improve their ability to pay by increased freight rates according to a formula which the royal commission was to recommend.
Where is the money going to come from? Is the Minister of Transport going to bring down another estimate of $40 million, or whatever amount is required to pay these increased wages, or will the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation be implemented by way of subsidies? Those are earmarked for a specific purpose. So the question immediately arises whether the one will be used to satisfy the other. Nothing of what was recommended by the Prime Minister on November 30 has happened. The royal commission did not produce a formula, and the railways will have to pay the wage increases from the subsidies they will receive from the government for this particular purpose or for other purposes.
The Prime Minister in the speech he made the other day over the air on the program "The Nation's Business" tried to create the impression that the Liberal party last fall was opposed to government action in order to prevent a strike. That statement is simply untrue. We said again and again last fall that we were against a railway strike, but instead of accepting the mere delaying tactics proposed by the government at that time we said, in the form of an amendment-and it is there for anyone to see-that the strike could be prevented through a settlement based on the Milvain report, and that is exactly what has happened.

The question I asked while the Prime Minister was absent from the house was, when are we going to get a statement of policy from the government with reference to this whole matter, the report of the royal commission and the four recommendations that were made and the policy of the government with reference to the manner in which funds will be provided for the settlement of the strike?
I think the committee is entitled to know and the country is entitled to know. We have not heard a word, and that is why I say,

These questions have been asked and the answer has been, "Well the committee will be set up and questions can be answered during the deliberations of that committee." While we do know that there has been deterioration in the position of many Canadian National employees, there is on the order paper a resolution indicating that the directors will be increased from seven to 12. We will be dealing with that resolution on another occasion. While there are hundreds of thousands of people out of work in this country, there is on the order paper a resolution indicating that the number of directors of the Canadian National Railways is going to be increased. How many people have been laid off by the Canadian National? What is the position of the employees at the McGill street headquarters of Canadian National Railways and the aviation building in Montreal?
I attempted to move the adjournment of the house on one occasion to deal with this situation. The minister made the usual statement that, in so far as the Canadian National Railways were concerned, they were not interested in laying off people; they would do the best they could. I think the minister owes it to these people to say what is the position of those men who are employed in the headquarters building of Canadian National Railways at 360 McGill street and the adjoining building and who, because of the shift from that building to the new office premises in the city of Montreal, may be laid off. What is the position of those who are engaged in the maintenance of those buildings, now that Canadian National Railways are handing out this work to a contractor? How many of these men remain out of work? In the C.N.R. building alone 160 of them were affected by this move, and I am told that in the aviation building a number were also affected.
This first item should not be allowed to pass, Mr. Chairman, until the committee is given the details. I will give the minister credit for this sentiment. I am sure that he is not any more anxious than anybody else to see men out of work. But that feeling will not suffice. What is the position of these people who have lost their jobs. Before this first item is disposed of I hope the minister will be able to tell us what the situation is.

That is another reason we should have a complete breakdown of the position as it affects these employees.
I next come to the question of aviation services. I am somewhat surprised that a statement has not been made by the government with reference to aviation policy in Canada. I do not believe a statement has been made on aviation policy for many years. Certainly no statement has been made by the present government except, of course, in answer to questions that were put to the former minister of transport and to others. I do not think that is a healthy situation, Mr. Chairman. Because the air services in any country are of such great importance, careful consideration should be given to the position having to do first with (1) international carriers; (2) domestic and transcontinental carriers; and (3) regional carriers. No announcement of policy has been made. I submit to the minister that he should give some indication of what the policy is.
I should like to say a word in connection with the bilateral air agreements. There are in existence a number of bilateral air agreements that Canada has made with other countries. Since this government has been in office those agreements have been detrimental to Canada. They have been detrimental because Canada has given away certain of its sovereign rights-I refer to fifth freedom rights-to foreign carriers when Canada itself did not have those rights in the foreign countries concerned. In one case Canada gave up a substantial and important right in its own country in an exchange with another country.
There has been or there is before the cabinet an application by Canadian Pacific Airlines for certain international air services. In equity and in fairness I think the committee is entitled to know the nature of the application and the government's decision on it. Surely the government is not going to sit on it. What are the demands that are made in the international field by Canadian Pacific Airlines? Have Trans-Canada Air Lines made similar representations? What has been the decision of the government? Is the government still studying those applications?
Under the Aeronautics Act-I have forgotten the section, but I believe it is section 15

-it falls within the jurisdiction of the governor in council to deal with applications of that nature when the applicant is also a surface carrier. What is the position of carriers in so far as transcontinental services are concerned? Have Canadian Pacific Airlines made application for certain services? Will those applications be dealt with by the cabinet, or will they be given to the air transport board for determination?
It would seem to me that the logical body to make a determination on applications of that kind is the air transport board. They are a technical body. They have all the necessary facilities. They have held hearings from one end of the country to the other. Last year, during consideration of the estimates of the minister's predecessor, a statement was made that regional hearings were being held by the air transport board all across Canada, first in the eastern part of Canada and later in the western part, and that some decisions would be arrived at. It seems to me that the committee is entitled to know what those decisions are.
Then again there is the question of the regional air carriers. Need I tell the minister that some of them are in difficult circumstances and need assistance? Perhaps all of them need assistance. I know definitely of some instances, in the province of Quebec particularly, where assistance is needed if the carrier is to be able to carry on.

There was little secret that the A.I.T.A. members were dissatisfied with Mr. Balcer's defence of the controversial decontrol policy and more forthright indignation was only suppressed by the members' consideration for the fact that he has just stepped into the post of a new minister.
Following that up, may I say that the minister was told that in 1958 the aviation industry employed about 40,000 people directly and 65,000 people indirectly, and was the third largest employer in Canada. In 1960, for which I have the latest figures, the

It was taken for granted-and in fact it was so stated at the A.I.T.A. conference in Quebec-that the position in 1960 would be worsening.
The Prime Minister asked me to what air carrier I referred. I refer to an article which appeared in L'Echo du Bas Saint-Laurent, in which it is stated that Quebecair is being threatened because of competition from other carriers, but more particularly T.C.A. Many reasons are given in the article, but I will only place this paragraph on record. I think it is an excellent article; the minister may have seen it. (Translation):
The Quebec Airways, or Quebecair, has struggled mightily to secure the right of flying the Quebec airlanes. The company is using those airlanes as its natural field of operations. There is therefore no valid reason for T.C.A. to continue duplicating Quebecair service between Montreal and Seven Islands. We have it from good authority that, if Quebecair had the monopoly of its airway network, they could give first class service and prosper. On the other hand, if T.C.A. keeps competing, this state-owned company will pile up deficits and, which is still worse, jeopardize the survival of Quebecair, a private enterprise.
(Text):
I do not, of course, intend to extend the same arguments to other corporations having to do with T.C.A. This being a regional area I think the position is entirely different than that of the two main carriers in this country, namely, T.C.A. and C.P.A. But I hope the government is taking into consideration the recommendations of its own report, the Wheatcroft report, and I trust the minister has given consideration to the conclusions which were reached by the distinguished commissioner which at the request of the government made a complete study of the whole field. It was clear, following that report, that there should not be competition in certain areas, and that when competition did take place it was to happen in a very gradual way. Particular reference was made to a five year period and a ten year period. I have forgotten the date of the Wheatcroft report, but I think it was published some three or four years ago.
However, having regard to the deficit of Trans-Canada Air Lines, which amounted to $2J million in 1960, and the deficit of the Canadian Pacific Airlines, amounting to $4

million or more during the same period, the government, it seems to me, must be extremely careful in reaching any decision which it might make either in the international field or in the domestic and transAtlantic fields which would affect the strength of either of those two great corporations.
That is easier said than done. I will grant at once that in theory it is easy, in the field of aviation, to make a general statement, but when you come to apply it things are far more difficult. That is why I say this is not a political question. It is a technical question which should be decided on the merits and the facts, and there is a body which deals with that responsibility under the Aeronautics Act, namely the air transport board.

Yes, the particular application as between T.C.A. and C.P.A. had to do with domestic air cargo, but the decision the government took was made following a study by the air transport board after a hearing before them, and its effect had to do with international services and international air cargo as well. That is why I say to the minister that it seems to me this whole question is one for a technical body, the air transport board, which has the facilities and the personnel to deal with this matter in the manner in which it should be handled. If it is dealt with by that body, and if there is a recommendation made, I do not think the minister will find any exception being taken from this side of the house.
I should like just to say one word about the shipping policy which the minister announced yesterday in the House of Commons. I told him, and I repeat, that in my opinion it was one of the most important statements to have been made in this house in a very long time. It has to do with three aspects of water transportation; assistance to the shipping operator and the shipbuilder; assistance to the fishing industry; and cabotage, or the manner in which ships may move in and out of the great lakes.
The minister has stated that the first two aspects will not be dealt with by legislation, but brought about by means of an item to be introduced in the estimates. In so far as the latter item is concerned, namely the one involving amendment to the commonwealth merchant shipping agreement, there is a point which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister.
My recollection is that there are five kinds of trade on the great lakes. There is trade moving from one Canadian port to another Canadian port; there is trade moving from one United States port to another United

States port; there is trade moving from a Canadian port to a United States port; there is trade moving from a Canadian port to an overseas port, and there is trade moving from a United States port to an overseas port. As the situation is now, the laws of the United States prevent or prohibit cabotage or the carrying by foreign vessels of trade or cargo from one United States port to another United States port.	[DOT]
This is not so in Canada. That restriction does not apply to British vessels or to commonwealth vessels. They may move from one Canadian port to another Canadian port, and the announcement the minister made yesterday was that he intends to apply for an amendment to the act so that after the passage of that act, cabotage, as I call it, will not be permitted to other than Canadian vessels in that area from Les Escoumains to the head of the lakes. Downstream from Les Escoumains, British vessels and commonwealth vessels will be able to trade from one Canadian port to another Canadian port. The question that comes to my mind therefore, is this. What will be the position, first, of Canadian owners who are now operating vessels under the British flag; and what will be the position of Canadian owners who have transferred their flag to other flags of convenience, as did the operator I referred to yesterday? Does this mean that they will bring their ships back to the Canadian flag?
The next question I should like to ask the minister is this. He has already stated that he intends to amend the shipping act in order to bring this about, and I think there is a part of the shipping act which has to do with this matter; but will that be done only after an agreement has been completed with the commonwealth countries? If that is so, does the minister anticipate that agreement with the commonwealth countries can be finalized before the end of this session? This must be an international agreement, an intercommonwealth agreement, and I take it these agreements are not made overnight but by representations on a formal basis through the usual offices, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, or by meetings of a committee.
What effect is this policy going to have on the ships of the Canadian National Steamships line that are still lying at anchor in Halifax harbour? Will it be possible to use this policy, in some form or other, to assist those ships? Have payments been made in accordance with the agreement that has been arrived at between the Browning company and the guarantors through the bank of Cuba, and has the new bank repudiated any of the payments? Will the minister give consideration to rehabilitating these ships under the

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should have begun my remarks with some acknowledgement of the pleasure it is to be speaking in the House of Commons on Saturday. It seems to have been such a popular move, particularly with the staff although they seem to have shared an inordinate amount of credit for the condition, that I should like to extend my words of appreciation to those hon. members who have managed to find it possible to be here on this particular day.
The theme on which I should like to approach the estimates of the Department of Transport and the whole question of transportation has really been offered to us by the Prime Minister in his ringing declaration that the future election, which I think most of us will agree will be coming very soon, is going to be centred on the issue of free enterprise versus socialism. I know this is a topic that is dear to many members' hearts, particularly on the government side, and I want to try to analyse the problems that we face in transportation in the light of this situation.
If the issue is between free enterprise and socialism, it seems to me that in all fairness the thing to do is to get the government out of any kind of operation of transportation services at all. If you are going to have a pure and thus, I think, a practical free enterprise approach, if you are going to use the theme that as a political party and government you stand for free enterprise, then it seems to me that the challenge is to get the government out of any kind of transportation operation. That is the first point.
How do you get the government out of such operations? Do you sell the C.N.R.? Do you sell Northern Transportation Limited? Do you turn them over to private enterprise? That is one side of the problem. The other question is, what about the problem of subsidies? If you are a free enterpriser and against socialism, especially the creeping or dead hand of socialism, are you going to offer subsidies to private enterprise in any shape or form?
Yesterday we had an announcement, which will be very much welcomed in my own region and is welcomed by this party, in relation to the shipbuilding industry. But I put it to the minister and to the Conservative members of the house: In view of the Prime Minister's theme for the next election, does this announcement not bother you? Does it not strike a blow at the very purity of your theme of free enterprise? The minister was candid enough to say that there is no idea what this is going to cost. I know that last
[Mr. Hellyer.i
year the hon. member for Laurier and I made recommendations along this line and he estimated the cost, as I remember, at $40 million to $50 million a year to carry out this kind of proposal, that is, a 40 per cent contribution to the capital cost and a fitting in with the depreciation pattern we already have.
It seems to me that there is here a challenge to the government to explain to us how this announcement, which I take as a form of socialism, fits into the free enterprise theme. After all, if you are going to underwrite both the shipyards and the shipbuilding industry to the extent of 40 per cent of capital costs, you will have a most difficult time coming forward as an apostle of free enterprise. This is something in a policy way that I wish the minister would explain. How does this announcement that we welcome fit in with the role of the government in moving from this trend toward socialism toward what the Prime Minister says is the issue in the next election?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Would he call the United States government a socialist government because it gives subsidies to its shipping and shipyard operations?

No, I would suggest that throughout the world we have a trend toward both planning and the support of industries by governments. I was talking to a Conservative just before I came into the chamber who was telling me how attracted he was-I think this is fair-to the statements of senator Barry Goldwater and the whole idea of stopping the trend toward collectivism and the mixed economy. Is this theme of free enterprise versus socialism going to be an attempt to stop the trend toward collectivism and the mixed economy? In all fairness, I think the minister has to recognize that this is a trend toward a mixed economy. Here is a 40 per cent underwriting of the shipbuilding industry and the shipping industry in Canada.
I also hope that some time during this debate Conservative members from the west, especially those representing prairie constituencies where grain is shipped, will give us their views on the announcement of yesterday. I acknowledge there is a tradition, whether you are a Conservative, Liberal or C.C.F.'er from the west, that you want the cheapest shipping rates possible in order to get your grain into foreign markets, and

I should like to hear from these western members whose constituents export grain as to what they feel the effect will be.
Will the hon. member permit a question? Where are the C.C.F. members from the west?

Where are the C.C.F. members from the west? I was referring to C.C.F. members who have been here in the past. We have one C.C.F. member from the west now and I think we are likely to have more again. That is beside the point. I should like to hear what the western members think of this announcement and what it may do to the cost of carrying their grain to world markets.
I want to touch on another aspect of this question of free enterprise versus socialism. We have had the argument put forward in other places attached to this house that the government should get out of the operation of Northern Transportation Limited. Here is a company that is not really making money and it is in competition with private enterprise, so the theme is get rid of it and let private enterprise handle the freight transportation problem in the Yukon. We have a situation with the Polymer Corporation where a crown organization is making a great deal of money and the argument there seems to be that we should sell it right away because what business does the government have in engaging in any field in which money can be made? This is another contradiction in the free enterprise approach of the present government that I cannot understand.
There is in Canada today a free enterpriser who has spoken forth recently and who seems to have a certain amount of influence with the government. I am referring to Mr. Crump, the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Not long ago on the occasion of the annual meeting of the Canadian Pacific, he made an address that was well covered in the press. I should like to quote an extract from the Gazette of May 4, 1961. Mr. Crump sets out a number of the difficulties confronting the Canadian economy at the moment, and points out that the growth of the gross national product per capita does not match that of the United States. Then, he says this:
Among the reasons responsible for this undesirable situation, it would appear, is that Canada, to a greater degree than the United States, is committed to the mixed economy, in which state enterprise and private enterprise function in coexistence.
I can only take that statement as a criticism of the mixed economy. I should like to hear the minister's views because, as I understand it, Mr. Crump's air line has been before 90205-6-302J
Supply-Transport
him and before the cabinet in relation to demands that it have a better break, as a private enterprise carrier, in the carriage of passengers.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Would he explain a little further why he took that as a criticism on the part of Mr. Crump? I have read the statement but I did not take it as a criticism.
The hon. member is mistaken. I did not say this was a criticism of the Prime Minister.
I thought the hon. member said it was a criticism of the mixed economy?

Yes. Well, he set out why Canada is not doing so well. He said that among the reasons responsible for this undesirable situation it would appear is that Canada, to a greater degree than the United States, is committed to the mixed economy in which state enterprise and private enterprise function in co-existence. I can only take it from that that Mr. Crump thinks the mixed economy has gone too far. It is one explanation of why we are in a stagnation period.
When I undertook to question the statement I must say I had forgotten Mr. Crump's full statement. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member.

This is a legitimate line that Mr. Crump took. It is a legitimate line, but I do not agree with it, and his action in having Mr. McConachie down here lobbying for an extension of the franchise of Canadian Pacific Air Lines is in agreement with this particular attitude.
What I want to know is whether or not it is the attitude of the government that the mixed economy has gone too far. I know the Prime Minister was probably oversimplifying when he said the choice is going to have to be between free enterprise and socialism. Nowhere will you find a department in which you have this problem staring you right in the face to a greater extent than you do in the Department of Transport. I should like to give some examples.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
The hon. member has used the term "mixed economy". Will he define it?

Well, I do not want to get into a discussion of terminology, but I do not want

Supply-Transport
to use a term upon which there is some misunderstanding. Let us put it this way: It is an economy in which there is a great interrelationship between private business and government, where the government not only gives the initiative in certain fields but also gives subsidies and, in certain areas it carries on operations and services that could be carried on by private enterprise.
However, I wanted to point out some examples of this problem. I am sure every member of this house received a communication from the representatives of the trucking industry after the announcement was made that subsidies were going to be paid to the railways as a result of the MacPherson commission report-at least, we assume they are. The trucking industry, on the basis of the argument by the MacPherson commission that they are prime, hard, legitimate competitors of the railways, ask what business the government has in subsidizing the railways in competition with them. Again, they have a point if you accept the commission's attitude.
What is their thesis? As I understand it, it can be taken two ways. One of their positions is that they do not want the government subsidizing the railways at all. Let us say we are talking in terms of the relevant period. Their other argument, as I understand it, is, if you are going to subsidize the railways then you have to subsidize us. Of course, the railways and the railway unions answer by saying that the truckers are already subsidized by the fact that their right of way is provided by the taxpayers. You can get lost in this kind of maze. My argument is that we are going to have a blurring of the line between free enterprise and socialism.
One of the aspects upon which I expected the minister to comment, as he was requested to do by the hon. member for Laurier, is this question of air line competition. Perhaps I can best make my point by quoting from an article that appeared in the Montreal Star of May 6, 1961 under the heading "Air line costs cause fear of another 'C.N.R. situation' ". The article goes on to say:
Fear of "producing another C.N.R. situation" has become a dominating shadow hanging over the government's consideration of aviation policy, highly reliable sources said here today.
The fears have been heightened, these sources continued, by an estimate produced within the government that too rapid an increase in competition in the air could quickly send this country's air line losses up to around $40 million a year. The combined losses of Trans-Canada Air Lines and Canadian Pacific Airlines last year were $7 million.
If I could skip through the general argument and come to the last paragraph which is relevant to the request I should like to make of the minister, it reads:

The position of the Prime Minister on these issues appears to be unknown to his colleagues in the cabinet and is accepted as vital. External affairs minister Howard Green is widely identified as McConachie's strongest supporter in the cabinet. Finance minister Fleming, justice minister Fulton, trade minister Hees and transport minister Balcer are described as strongly opposed to granting the C.P.A. request at the present time.
This last paragraph is pure speculation. I introduce it only to suggest that, in this kind of situation which is being aggravated by these speculative stories, we deserve a statement from the minister on this particular issue. I would challenge him to come out with a free enterprise stand such as that which is going to be presented to the people at the next election. It seems to me the free enterprise stand should be to give Canadian Pacific whatever they want. If you are going to be a free enterpriser you have to widen the opening in the gates for competition. Let me underline the fact that this is not our position. It seems to me that in a battle between free enterprise and socialism, this is what you have to do. I expect before this debate is over we will hear from the minister what the free enterprise position of the government is in relation to this issue.
One other point upon which the minister did not touch to any great degree is the situation with regard to the St. Lawrence seaway and the fact that the seaway has not been bringing in the amount of revenue which had been estimated. The minister is aware that there is still a very strong feeling in certain parts of Canada, particularly in the Welland-Niagara area, that tolls on the seaway at the present time are discouraging traffic through the canal. There are still demands that tolls, in so far as Canada is concerned, should be wiped out. In essence, if you abolish tolls, you would be putting the government in the position of completely underwriting a service and getting no return from the private users of that service.
In one sense I suppose this is a denial of government intervention or the mixed economy. In another way, we need an explanation from the minister as to what the views of the government are. Again, as has so often happened in Canadian history, the government has taken the lead in providing a service and that service, in terms of return, does not match what was expected so we, as taxpayers, are underwriting the venture. What is the consistent approach, if you are going to provide a service like that? It seems that we would be on much better ground if we forgot about the tolls, and if we looked at services such as the St. Lawrence canal as vital to providing a traffic condition in the

country that we have needed to keep improving since a time prior to confederation and then to accept the fact that is a basic service that must be provided for.
From the canal situation I turn to what I think is a most expensive future aspect of transportation services as it relates to air. If any hon. members look at the charts at the back of the annual report of the department, I think they will note the astronomical rate of ascent of the expenses for air services and there is no indication at all that we have any horizon in sight. The cost is tremendous. This matter is having repercussions, but again the minister did not mention it in his address as far as I know. I refer him here to an article in the Financial Post of April 29 of this year which reads "Airlines pile up moans at cost of D.O.T. services".
The minister knows that D.O.T. is having difficulty in collecting from foreign air lines for the services we are providing. These services are tremendously expensive. When one looks at the aspects of meteorological services and telecommunications and realizes that as the jet age advances they are going to become more prosperous, I should like to ask again this question: Where is the free enterprise versus socialism philosophy in this matter? How do you adopt a free enterprise versus socialism philosophy and yet continue to go on providing these tremendously expensive services and extensions of services for what is in essence a fairly small sector of the country and a fairly small sector of the travelling public? It is this kind of paradox which makes this department a particularly fruitful field for inquiry on the basis of free enterprise or socialism or a middle of the road mixed economy. What are we getting into with the spiralling transportation costs in terms of the ethic that the Prime Minister has announced for his party? I think we deserve some kind of statement on this matter.
I would imagine that the costs in the next ten years would be well over $1 million just for air services and for those ancillary things that are required. I am sure we can afford this amount and I am sure these things should be provided. But when you provide this sort of thing, is it fair to accept the argument of Mr. Grant McConachie that Canadian Pacific Airlines deserve a chance to compete for and to get their share of the business in air travel? The Lord knows that the return one gets, whether it is from T.C.A. or C.P.A. or any other line, for the provision of services is just a pittance. I ask any hon. member to look at the fees which the Department of Transport gets from the provision of air services as against the expenditures. I refer
Supply-Transport
not only to the capital expenditures which are growing but also to the expenditures required just to keep the services in existence. No one would want to contend that we should go back to the horse and buggy days. Neither do we wish to restrict the development of these services. However, we need to see the provision of these services against the background of this free enterprise cry of the C.P.A.
One thing about Mr. Crump's announcement that intrigued me was this. If any hon. member looks at the historical review of the Canadian Pacific Railway as provided by the dominion bureau of statistics he will see in there a number of items which indicate that the C.P.R. has had provided over a number of years a tremendous amount of subsidy from the Canadian people both in terms of money and in terms of resources that were turned over to the railway. This fact again highlights the continuing dilemma in Canadian transport: What do you do from a free enterprise point of view or from a mixed economy point of view or from a socialistic point of view? I suggest that there is a great inconsistency in any political party that stands for free enterprise and yet continues to go along in the way in which the minister went yesterday with his announcement that we are going to underwrite 40 per cent of the cost of ships built in Canada.
One of the other aspects of which I thought the minister would treat is the following which I know is a delicate matter. No one wants to talk about this matter really and yet we have a very definite trend. I refer to the matter of winter transportation in the St. Lawrence river. I am sure the minister has seen the story in yesterday's Financial Post relating to the excitement of the gulf ports such as Baie Comeau and other ports like it, over the fact that their winter shipping is going ahead by leaps and bounds.
We know that there are now icebreakers and mechanical devices which can keep the port of Montreal open for almost the whole of the year. We also know that this is a delicate political problem because it is going to have its repercussions and its effects upon Halifax and Saint John. Yet I had a figure given to me by a man who is very prominent in shipping. He pointed out to me that the average saving per ton on freight coming through Halifax and Saint John in the winter as against that coming through Montreal is $12 a ton in favour of Montreal. One only has to look at the amount of freight coming through the two maritime ports in order to realize that we are in effect subsidizing the Atlantic ports by not pushing very strongly a policy to open up Montreal to winter

Supply-Transport
shipping. Again, there are political situations that need to be accounted for. But how can a free enterprise party continue to allow this kind of lack of efficiency to go on? I refer to shipping that costs $12 more a ton in effect to bring the goods to the Canadian people through an important part of the year when there are techniques and ships that can keep Montreal an open port.
One of the problems that always comes to mind in transportation as against other problems which the government faces relates to the matter of jurisdiction. That is one of the great excuses for all of us as politicians. I am sure every hon. member has been struck by this fact. If you are making a speech and somebody nails you with a question there is always a certain amount of delight in being able to say that this is really a matter for the provinces, and you can shrug off the responsibility. This just happens to be a department in which, except for the field of trucking, there is very little chance to shrug off anything because of the jurisdictional angle. For that reason it seems to me that this department, perhaps more than any other one, gives the government the opportunity to work out a coherent transportation policy for all parts of the national picture.
In that regard I should like to say this to the hon. member who suggested that the department be broken up-at least that is what I understood him to say-that it is really too big for any one man to administer. This is an argument that I have placed twice before the House of Commons in previous years and I am beginning to have doubts about it now. I am wondering if what we do not need is perhaps some more deputy ministers within this department or perhaps under ministers and then to have the minister in charge of transportation doing the job of trying to relate all the shipping and transportation problems we have in Canada; then have some five year or 10 year plan that will set objectives, set the amount of money we wish to spend and work out the amalgam we are going to have between private bodies and public bodies.
To me it is a striking thing that the royal commission on transportation really is not a royal commission on transporation but is just a royal commission on railways. I notice that a great many people have taken from the report of this royal commission that it stresses competition as the main factor in existence today within the transportation business. This is so. But one needs to underline the fact that this is competition between types of carrier services and not basically competition between carriers themselves. I

can see in our transportation picture no efficacy of cutthroat competition between the carriers themselves.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but I must inform him that his time has expired.
Go on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the committee give consent to the hon. member continuing?
Agreed.
Ten minutes.

I should only be another few minutes.
The competition which the transportation commission stresses is one which seems to me has some imperfection to it, as far as the government approach is concerned, because if we do not make some decision as to what is the best kind of service in certain areas we are going to have to have a dual service in which the various elements are rivalling each other. We can see this between T.C.A. and C.P.A.; we can see it between the various trucking companies. The approach to a solution, it seems to me, would be for the Minister of Transport to take as his goal some kind of integration of the transportation picture within a five year or a ten year plan and explain to Canadian citizens where we are going in transportation and how much it is going to cost.
I should like to offer one opinion on the matter and that is we should not be scared of either of these things; we should not be scared of this free enterprise idea and deciding that we are going to sell all government enterprises off. At the same time I do not think that in the trucking field we should go forward with the conception of underwriting all these truckers and, in effect, building up some kind of naturalized industry. It seems to me that in the next ten years what we need is some idea of our goal and how we are going to get there, and some lessening of the duplication we have. It seems to me that one thing which is required immediately is the bringing together of the transport industry within the ambit of the board of transport commissioners and some kind of integration between the various transport commissions we have at the present time. I am thinking of the national energy board, the board of transport commissioners, the air transport board and the Canadian maritime commission.
