Mr. Chairman, first of all, I should like to place some emphasis upon an area close to Montreal which would, at the outset, be the principal beneficiary of the modernization of the Richelieu canal system. For convenience in discussion, I have given this area the title of the "Canadian golden triangle".
I should point out that this title is now in use in the United States. For many years the name has been given to a tongue of land in the city of Pittsburgh, which is bounded on both sides by the Alleghany and Monon-gahela rivers, which join to become the Ohio river, thereby forming a triangular peninsula which is called the "golden triangle" by reason of the fact that the aforesaid tongue of land is completely covered by skyscrapers without a blade of grass in sight and is very comparable to the lower tip of Manhatten island, New York. It is hardly necessary for me to point out that the fabulously wealthy city of Pittsburgh is-besides having other distinctions-the steel capital of the entire world.
I have, therefore, given this name to an area of land on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river just opposite Montreal which is roughly triangular in shape and bounded on three sides by: (1) the St. Lawrence river from Sorel to Laprairie, or Candiac; (2) the Richelieu river from Sorel to St. Jean d'Iberville; (3) the area between Laprairie and St. Johns.
This area is what I have designated as the "golden triangle" of Canada, and I shall clearly demonstrate how richly deserved this appellation will be in a very few years' time. It will qualify as the greatest concentration of industrialization in all Canada. May I be allowed to state here, Mr. Chairman, that the
IMr. Johnson.]
beautiful towns of Chambly, Fort Chambly, Richelieu and St. Mathieu are located in the heart of this triangle.
It is doubtful if a high percentage of the citizens of our Canadian metropolis are aware that over 14 per cent of the population of this country live in greater Montreal, and with no decrease in the tempo at which their population, industrial expansion and building construction are assuming progressively larger proportions. The transformation presently taking place on Dorchester boulevard in Montreal, is a sufficient indication of things to come, and proves that Canada's largest city is now bursting at the seams, and for some years has been obliged to search for suitable factory sites far beyond the city limits.
Montreal has the principal car shops and other major installations in Canada for the servicing and reconditioning of the rolling stock of our two railways. Its new international airport has facilities second to none on the continent, it is Canada's principal seaport and has now embarked upon an era of terrific industrial expansion. But where? Not to the west of the island of Montreal where expansion is circumscribed by several non-navigable streams and inferior transportation and service facilities. Nor would expansion northwards toward the foothills of the Laurentian be attractive because of increasing remoteness from the facilities of the port of Montreal, and also because of inadequate rail communication. East of Montreal on the Quebec mainland, lies a large strip of somewhat desolate farmland with no sizeable municipality between Montreal and Three Rivers. There would be no adequate provision for housing for factory workers.
Actually the port of Montreal has recently extended its jurisdiction to cover an additional 25 miles downstream along the north shore, but solely in order to ensure that no new waterfront construction will hinder the future development of Montreal navigation and port facilities, which already have reached the saturation point. Some people have emphasized the fact that it will be many years before there is any perceptible change in the Montreal harbour picture downstream from the city. It is, therefore, very obvious that the logical extension of Canada's largest seaport can take place only on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, an area which has none of the disqualifications that characterize the other three major areas to the north, east and west.
Furthermore, shipment of merchandise manufactured in industrial plants situated to the north, east or west of Montreal can only

reach the harbour after the usual annoying delays encountered because of the serious traffic problem in this metropolis, for which no alleviation appears to be in sight. Contrariwise, the situation is becoming worse.
Implementation of the Richelieu canal modernization project should, of course, be a highly desirable concomitant to the utilization of the south shore or the extension of the port of Montreal facilities. The physical aspects of the canal project are briefly these; to deepen the present Richelieu canal, which now has only a depth of six feet and is about 100 years old, to 26 feet, the same as the seaway and, the construction of a new 15 miles of canal from Longueuil to Friar's island or from Laprairie basin, if the route from Sorel to St. Johns through the Richelieu river itself proves to be not economic or not logically possible. This canal, when completed, will provide the third side of the golden triangle. Two entrances will thus be available for United States bound traffic; (a) one at Sorel, Quebec, to handle upriver traffic from Seven Islands, Three Rivers, Port Cartier, European ports, etc. This would be a short route for iron ore shipments from new Quebec and Labrador, and newsprint from Three Rivers where the world's largest pulp and paper mills are situated, destined for New York city, which consumes one million tons of newsprint annually. And (b), the Longueuil entrance to the canal to be used for shipment to and from Montreal, the upper St. Lawrence and great lakes ports.
Admittedly, implementation of the canal project would be extremely costly, but as well as lower shipping costs for Canadian products to United States markets, commensurate benefits would similarly transform the economy of three large United States industrial states, New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania.
It will be noted that I respectfully recommend the deepening of the waterway to 26 feet-the same as the seaway. Already Lieutenant Colonel Lucien Dansereau, a member of the international joint commission, has indicated that he, having made an intensive study of the project, as well as official Washington, would recommend that we go along, as of now, on a basis of a 12-foot depth of the canal, but I feel that if the costly undertaking were justified at all, it should have the same depth as the seaway. I feel we should adopt that position rather than compromising on the 12 feet and then, I am sure, having all the expense of a further inevitable deepening in years to come.
It will be readily seen that a 440 mile waterway between Montreal and New York, instead of the 1,670 mile trip down the St. Lawrence, around the Gaspe peninsula and
Supply-Transport
thence along the Atlantic coast, would represent an enormous saving in transportation charges on many millions of tons of waterborne freight, annually.
I should like now to make reference to the hazards of the Atlantic route during war time. An aspect of this question that we cannot possibly afford to ignore concerns the effect that another world war would have upon the safety of our Atlantic communications. One of the latest editions of Janes' "Fighting Ships" published in London-conceded to be the leading authoritative reference for all statistical information concerning the navies of the world-claims that soviet Russia has 500 submarines available for Atlantic service, an undisclosed number of which are nuclear propelled and equipped with the latest in armaments. Janes do not exclude the possibility that certain of these submarines will be able to fire ballistic missiles without surfacing. R.V.B. Blackman editor of Janes, says:
In the event of hostilities, the allied navies might be threatened by 450 to 500 submarines, and the damage they could inflict on our material, personnel and economy staggers the imagination, when it is remembered that at the height of world war II, a little more than a fifth of this total were enough to bring the United Kingdom to the brink of starvation; not only as regards food for Britain's population, but as regards the vital raw materials required to prosecute the war.
Janes further believe that Russian submarines could seal off all communications between Europe and America, and it is well known that Soviet underwater craft have been caught making reconnaissances in the gulf of St. Lawrence, off the American Atlantic coast, and the coast of Argentina as well. We now live in a very small world.
The exposed Atlantic route would accordingly not be available for iron ore shipments from Port Cartier and Seven Islands once a world war got under way. So a short, deep water, sheltered route of 450 miles only between Montreal and New York is an absolute must.
Incidentally, Rear Admiral H. F. Pullen, flag officer, Atlantic coast and commander of the Atlantic submarine area under NATO, in a powerfully argued article appearing in the Atlantic Advocate of January, 1959 took a very pessimistic view of our defensive resources against the nuclear propelled Soviet submarines, some probably armed with ballistic missiles, which might even be capable of being launched by a submarine without surfacing.
Canada is not a member of the nuclear club; but we must agree that upon what success the western nuclear powers have in

Supply-Transport
establishing amicable relations with the communists will depend whether we have peace or war.
All the United States authorized groups and organizations, having either a geographical, economic or political interest in the implementation of the project, have been working feverishly to get the canal modernization under way, such as the state of New York, the state of Vermont, the joint state, New York and Vermont, commission on the Champlain basin, the port of New York authority and the United States army corps of engineers. Besides, the congressional delegation from both these states I mentioned have instructions from their state governments to place pressure on Washington to schedule an early commencement of the project.
There is little doubt in my mind, Mr. Chairman, that if the Kennedy administration can be persuaded that the short, modernized, sheltered waterway between Montreal and New York is absolutely necessary to over-all continental defence, Washington may not be inclined to take no as Ottawa's answer; there is too much at stake. The project was also strongly endorsed by Governor Nelson Rockefeller during his gubernatorial campaign. It is perhaps unfortunate that practically all of the physical and engineering aspects of the work lie in Canadian territory.
Let me return for a moment to the potentialities of the "golden triangle". Here are some highlights that were suggested by competent observers. It contains the entrance to the St. Lawrence seaway. It would contain all entrances to the proposed Richelieu canal. At this point let us not forget that the valley of the Richelieu river is the cradle of the Canadian nation. It is the hub of direct rail routes and highways connecting Montreal with (a) the eastern United States, wherein lies the greatest concentration of United States markets and industrialization; and (b) direct rail routes to the maritime provinces. The Steel Company of Canada is now operating its new $10 million plant at Contrecoeur. The Quebec Iron and Titanium Corporation has spent an additional $5 million on new plant facilities, making $80 million in all invested by this ambitious company in Quebec province. Thousands and thousands of new jobs are already available. Nationally known companies have allocated a total of $500 million for plant facilities in the area, either already completed, under construction or projected, with a potential of 70,000 industrial jobs on completion of the schedule.

Natural gas from western Canada is almost available in the triangle for industrial and residential purposes. The area is also serviced by the Shawinigan Water and Power Company or, rather, its subsidiary, the Southern Canada Power Company and Hydro-Quebec. The tonnage of two-way traffic anticipated for a modernized Richelieu canal would be comparable with, or even exceed, present traffic on the seaway.
Many homesites approved by the crown company, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, as well as by industrial plants for their workers, are under construction in the triangle to provide adequate housing commensurate with the projected industrial expansion. Schools, churches, recreation and shopping centres will follow in due course. A large part of the triangle will be only 20 minutes distant from downtown Montreal.
I repeat, the "golden triangle" a few years hence could conceivably become the greatest concentration of industrialization to be found anywhere in Canada. I would therefore express the hope that the government will endeavour by every means at its disposal to keep implementation of the canal project very much in mind.
It may not be out of place, Mr. Chairman, when discussing developments of properties, whether in industrial or residential districts, or in desolate areas where an abundance of valuable mineralization has been discovered, to recall that in August, 1958, when opening the Canadian National exhibition at Toronto, our Prime Minister made a vibrant appeal for acceleration in the exploitation of our fabulous hinterland, and he further drew attention to the startling fact that only 10 per cent of the total area of our country is privately owned, the remaining 90 per cent of our vast expansive territory consisting of crown lands being held either by federal or provincial governments.
Those who remind us that a sizeable percentage of this area is uninhabitable tundra or barren land in the far north do not take sufficient cognizance of the fact that we are living in the atomic age. I believe that certain nuclear physicists of impeccable professional reputation have even hinted that outdoor air conditioning, climate control, may well be within the range of future possibiliti-ties. This could hardly be more fantastic than the circumnavigation of the earth by a guided missile, already a "fait accompli".
Far too high a percentage of our native Canadians are completely indifferent as to the ownership of property, probably because Canada has more territory than she knows what

to do with. Most immigrants coming to Canada to seek homes and careers have been truly amazed at our general apathy when it comes to the acquisition of real estate. These new Canadians coming from the crowded countries of central or eastern Europe where every square foot of land has been chained down for centuries will often forgo the necessities of life in order to keep up their instalments on a piece of property in what they often call our undeveloped country.
What Canada needs more than anything else is a tremendous infusion of new wealth. We have at our back door the last natural treasure house left on the continent, with an abundance of valuable mineralization whose development is still in the early stages. Its exploitation should be accelerated as rapidly as the necessary capital and equipment can be obtained and, may I hope, primarily for Canadians.
Let me conclude, Mr. Chairman, with a reference to my own province. No government is perfect, but Quebec citizens have not entirely forgotten the achievements of the predecessor government of the province of Quebec for the benefit of Quebec agriculture and for the development of our superb natural resources as well as the massive industrialization program inaugurated and now attaining higher levels by leaps and bounds, and which will be crowned by the spectacular exploitation of the "golden triangle". There is no comparison between the transformation that has taken place in the economy of our province in recent years and contrariwise the lethargy and vacuum that characterized the Liberal regimes.
In point of history, Quebec is our oldest province and the intensive industrialization of the "golden triangle", not to mention new Quebec, will maintain the pre-eminence of the banner province for many years to come. Thank you.

and making a far-reaching change in our shipping policy. That change is not to be made in this important matter by the introduction of legislation in the House of Commons. Legislation has been introduced during this session on matters of far less importance than the matters which were dealt with by my hon. friend yesterday. On this occasion in respect of this extremely important and far-reaching change of policy, the government is going to proceed by way of item in the estimates rather than by way of legislation. The government is going to proceed not only by way of an item in the estimates but by a dollar item in the estimates, a procedure which they used to attack very bitterly in the past in respect of far less important matters than a change in Canadian shipping policy.
The minister has said that it is necessary or desirable to handle the matter in this way because no one knows how much money may be required. That is perfectly true, but it does not prevent the government from making an estimate of the amount of money that might be required and putting that amount in an estimate. Then if it is not sufficient, they can always get extra money in the next estimates. There is no reason in the world why the matter should be dealt with in this way or why parliament should not be given some idea of the general extent of the program. However, in connection with a change in Canadian ship policy which is of national and international importance, we now find that this government is going to proceed by putting a $1 item in the supplementary estimates.

The Leader of the Opposition has in part covered what I wished to say when I rose. I must admit that I cannot understand the attitude the government is taking to this most important matter. It will, of course, be realized that the statement made yesterday by the minister was on a most important matter. I simply cannot understand the approach that is being made by the minister and by the government.
The minister has within the last five minutes said that this matter is going to be covered by a supplementary vote of $1. That statement indicates to me that he does not know what the program is going to cost. Not knowing what it is going to cost, the government or the minister puts in the supplementary estimates an item of $1. However, he told us yesterday it meant 10,000 direct jobs in the shipbuilding industry and 10,000 indirect jobs. If the minister can tell us, as he

told us yesterday, that it means 20,000 jobs, he must have some idea of the cost to the government over and above the cost of $1.
I say quite bluntly that if the hon. member was not being political yesterday because there is a by-election in Esquimalt-Saanich and because there are two shipbuilding yards in Esquimalt-Saanich, then he must have some information about the cost. In addition to that, there is this consideration. I am certain that every member of this committee will vote any money required to rebuild the shipbuilding industry of Canada. But the way in which the minister is now presenting the matter to us means that the House of Commons is completely in the dark and that he is asking for a blank cheque. I do not believe in blank cheques, Mr. Chairman. I do not believe in the $1 item technique in this instance. Surely the minister can give us more information, more direction or be a little bit more specific. Surely he can act more in keeping with the integrity of a cabinet minister and not so much in keeping with expediency having regard to a by-election in Esquimalt-Saanich.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I think the document that I read yesterday stated in very clear fashion the shipping policy of this government to come to the rescue of the shipping and shipbuilding industries in this country which in the last 15 years have been left in an awful state by the previous government.
And the present government. Hon. members opposite have been in office for four years.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Yes; and we came up with something.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have been in office for four years and this policy was forecast six months ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: The shipbuilders and the ship operators understood what I said yesterday.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Parliament does not matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: What I said yesterday was that we wanted shipbuilding to have a chance to survive in Canada.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I think we are bringing in a measure that will really give us a place in the sun. What I said was very clear. We are giving a subsidy of 35 per cent on shipping built in Canada, to be registered under Canadian registry. This 35 per cent is given in order to provide an incentive. It will be put up to 40 per cent until March 31, 1963. In

addition, we intend to help the fishing industry in a manner which would give our fishermen a chance to compete with foreign trawlers operating near the coast of Canada. We intend to help the fishermen who are working in very small boats. We are going to look after them, too.
Boat construction?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: If the hon. member would read what I said yesterday he would not be so worried. We are not doing this only to please the people from Esquimalt-Saanich. We are doing what this government has always done. We are trying to answer the needs of the Canadian people in general and, in this instance, provide help for an industry which has known great days in the history of Canada. Canada has always built ships. This new policy has been extremely well received by the industry, by labour, and by the public in general. I am asking all hon. members to support the government when it comes before parliament with such forward looking legislation whose only purpose is to help Canadians to help themselves.

The minister has said that this policy is of extreme importance and will prove of great advantage to the people of Canada. We hope it will. When the time comes, we shall make our views clear with respect to that policy. The minister does not intend to proceed with respect to this policy by way of legislation. He says we can proceed by way of legislation with respect to a good many matters which are of less importance, but when we deal with shipping policy -a policy which the minister says will put the industry on a new foundation-we are to proceed by way of an item in the estimates.
The minister said we have to do it that way, irrespective of the rights and privileges of parliament, because we do not know how much money we shall have to spend. But the minister told us yesterday we know how much more employment will be created-that it was going to employ 10,000 people directly and 10,000 indirectly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

Nevertheless, my point is this: the minister has the details when it comes to the employment which may be created but when we ask him how much this might cost he says he has no idea, so we are to proceed by way of an item in the estimates. We have to put an item of $1 in the estimates. That item of $1 was something against which hon. members opposite used to inveigh when we on this side formed the government. Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to congratulate the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) for the decisively progressive policy he announced yesterday regarding coastal shipping in Canadian waters and shipbuilding.
With all due deference to opposition members who complain about this declared policy of the government, I am sure that it is an asset which will help solve the problem this industry is facing by improving the conditions in a field that has been neglected for many years by the previous administration.
I would like also to thank the minister for the kind support he gave me in all the representations made in connection with the Soulanges canal.
Last fall, at the request of the Vaudreuil-Soulanges voters, the minister was kind

enough to use his influence to hasten the work on the jetties which now replace the swing-bridges over the Soulanges canal.
At the request of these same people, the minister agreed to set aside part of the properties along the canal, which will be used as a lure to get the industries that have been needed for so long in that part of my constituency. In fact the establishment of industries there would provide profitable and stable employment in a section of my constituency.
Despite the province of Quebec offer to take over the whole Soulanges canal, which would have relieved him of a heavy task, the minister, with all his many occupations, worked overtime in the interest of a population which is grateful to him for his devotion. May I be allowed here to thank him for that, both in my own name and on behalf of my constituents. With reference to the offer made by the province of Quebec to take back all properties along the Soulanges canal, I must say that, at first glance, one must be more than a realist not to accept it at once, because the decisions to be taken will affect the economic future of a whole area. I believe we must, by all means possible, ensure the prosperity of an area that deserves to be developed. The minister of fisheries and game of the province of Quebec wishes to obtain all properties along Soulanges canal in order to set up there a fishbreeding centre and develop camping grounds and parks for tourists. We approve all those projects and we admire those who planned them.
That is why we have refused to sell any part of those lands to private individuals. We were keeping them for the department of game and fisheries of the province of Quebec.
However, it is feared in Vaudreuil-Sou-langes that the transfer of the canal to the provincial government will cause some trouble.
Over the past few months, hundreds of provincial employees who had lost their jobs have been replaced by supporters of the new party in power, as a result of directives from a group of patronage distributors.
The people of Vaudreuil-Soulanges would not want the plans worked out by the minister of games and fisheries of Quebec to be used only to reward those who voted for the party temporarily in power in Quebec.
I should like at this point to draw a comparison between what was done in Ottawa after the Conservatives were returned to office in 1957, and what has been going on since the Liberal party took over in Quebec last June.

Out of 600-odd federal civil servants resident in Vaudreuil-Soulanges, none have lost their jobs for showing a preference for any of the political parties represented in this house.
All employees who had been operating the Soulanges canal from the beginning have been able, through our efforts, to find other employment either on the St. Lawrence seaway or at Lachine or at Ste. Anne de Bellevue or elsewhere, or have been pensioned off.
The wholesale dismissals by the provincial government of workers who in fact had only exercised their rights as free citizens are not likely to improve relations with political opponents who have very different views on the way to deal with economic problems.
Such actions show a total lack of social sense and Christian charity. The Liberals should have shown greater wisdom and greater respect for the working classes of Quebec.
I feel duty bound to do everything in my power to protect from political retaliation on the part of the Quebec Liberal party, those free citizens whose only desire is to be able to earn an honest living.
Soulanges canal was built at the turn of the century for a specific purpose: to improve navigation between Montreal and the great lakes so that 14-foot draft ships could increase their cargoes between the two points.
It had never entered into the minds of the public men, of the economists and engineeers of that time to make it a fishpond or a tourist's paradise. Let the Quebec minister of game and fisheries think of turning it overnight into a hatchery, if he so wishes. Let him dream. But a canal, an economic instrument, cannot be altered into a centre for tourists and sportsmen without undergoing deep changes.
The Tory government is ready to let go of the most important section of the canal to serve this purpose. I refer to all the area west of Pointe Cascades extending for 13 miles in the direction of lake St. Francois and which includes:
1.	A strip approximately 200 feet wide all along the south side of the canal;
2.	About 10 acres of fine land and the power station at Coteau du Lac;
3.	A piece of land of about 60 acres between the canal and the C.N.R. line near Coteau du Lac;
4.	A large piece of land on the shore of lake St. Francois, at Coteau Landing; for which we refused $15,000;
5.	All the land north of the canal where the provincial department of roads built
Supply-Transport
highway No. 2 without having to pay anything for expropriation purposes. That is what the federal government is offering the department of game and fisheries for the fabulous amount of $1-referring to the amount of $1 mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson)-this is a genuine offer of $1-not to mention the $100,000 it cost the federal government last fall to replace the swing bridges.
If we were asking half a million dollars for all those properties, the minister, Hon. Gerard Levesque, woud be justified in haggling about it, but we are offering him without any charge more than 90 per cent of the Soulanges canal properties.
We want to offer industrialists and people who are looking for an ideal site to set up an industry of some kind or to expand their present industries, the Pointe Cascades sector which is connected to the seaway, only two miles away, by lake St. Francois. We merely wish to diversify sources of employment in the Soulanges district. We feel that that is a sounder policy, that it rests on better principles than if Soulanges had all its eggs in one basket, as the Liberals would have it. We are anxious to please the tourists but we feel that our main concern must be the working class which would find permanent employment in the district through the establishment of small and medium size industries.
A campaign has been going on in Quebec for some time now whose object is to have French Canadians get control of part of their economy. Many of our young people wish to set up their own industry, but cannot afford to have their meager capital engulfed in one swoop in the buying of expensive properties near the metropolis. Our suggestion meets their desires and, if implemented, would be of a great help to them.
Let the Quebec game and fisheries and trade and commerce departments agree on a proposal which would reserve Pointe Cascades or a certain area of the canal for the establishment of small Quebec industries, and we shall lose no time in concluding this business about the Soulanges canal. But we do not want to have them talk only of fishing and camping. Low wage earners too are entitled to their share in the development of the Quebec territory.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) stated this morning that he had some knowledge of the petitions of the Soulanges chambers of commerce urging that the entire Soulanges canal be surrendered to the province of Quebec. Well, Mr. Chairman, there

Supply-Transport
is only one chamber of commerce in the whole Soulanges area. However, there is an industrial development committee whose purpose, as its name indicates, is to promote the establishment of industries in Soulanges.
Having attended a number of meetings of the Soulanges chamber of commerce and of various organizations in the area, I am in a position to state that the people of Vaudreuil-Soulanges are now prepared to accept for lack of anything better, the scheme put forward by the Quebec department of game and fisheries. But if some industry expressed a desire to locate at Pointe Cascades or at the other end of Vaudreuil-Soulanges and was able to provide 200 or 300 permanent jobs, the whole population would support the new scheme.
Besides, the federal government has no
authority to promote any specific industrialization in any area of the country. There is no other means to encourage the establishment of industries in the Soulanges area than to announce that some crown buildings and lands, comprising the Soulanges canal property, shall be put up for sale, in accordance with departmental regulations and practices. In such a way, we shall know who is interested, what industries and investors wish to set up an industry in the Soulanges area. We shall know at the same time whether that area is suitable for industrial expansion.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me our action should inspire the Quebec legislators, and that instead of trying to confuse the issue and multiply promises, they should show more realism and begin by carrying out their fishbreeding project and creating that anglers' and tourists' paradise in the area we have offered them.

Mr. Chairman, I should now like to refer to another matter in respect of the Department of Transport in which I take great interest.
Having had the opportunity to meet members of the Canadian air lines pilots' association, I was shocked to learn how to what a marked extent our once dynamic aviation air lines industry, mainly Canadian Pacific Air Lines and Trans-Canada Air Lines, have lost business to their foreign competitors. This has had the result of forcing our major air lines to face the possibility of having to discharge nearly 100 pilots within the near future. The discharging of 100 pilots will result in approximately 1,000 jobs lost in hangars and airports, with a subsequent loss of employment for well paid technicians. It is pathetic to hear about the plight of professional pilots who will now have to emigrate to Europe in order to continue in their
[Mr. Bourbonnais.l
profession or abandon their profession and seek positions in inferior fields of employment. This same situation applies to thousands of skilled Canadian air lines' employees who will have to seek other sources of income.
This situation has been caused by an imbalance and weakness in the Canadian air lines as compared with the more aggressive foreign competitors on this continent and abroad. As an example of this I should like to cite a few facts regarding our major air lines' weakness in improving their methods in this field of transportation. I shall first list the routes from Canadian cities served unilaterally by foreign carriers. There exist over 2,000 miles Canadian-United States border between Toronto and Victoria, where no Canadian air line has scheduled transborder rights. This large area of Canada is served by five United States carriers, which are as follows: 1. Edmonton-Winnipeg-Min-neapolis-Chicago and the northwest; 2. Ed-monton-Calgary-Great Falls-Denver-Las Vegas and Los Angeles; 3. Regina-Minot, North Dakota and north central United States; 4. Calgary-Spokane-Portland, San Francisco and the west coast; 5. Vancouver direct to Seattle-San Francisco-Los Angeles. These areas are served by the following air lines respectively: Northwest Air Lines, Western Air Lines, North Central Air Lines, West Coast Air Lines and United Air Lines.
No Canadian air line has the right to serve the capital of the United States from either Ottawa, Toronto or Montreal or western Canada. This service is provided by Eastern Air Lines and Northwest Air Lines exclusively.
Another imbalance exists because no Canadian air line is allowed rights over the following major North American routes: Ottawa-Washington, Toronto-Washington, Montreal-Washington and western Canada-Washington, which are served by Eastern Air Lines, American Air Lines, Eastern Air Lines and Northwest Air Lines, respectively. This same imbalance exists between Montreal-Frankfurt and Montreal-Amsterdam, which are served by Lufthansa and K.L.M., respectively.
A comparison can be made between the United States and Canada in respect of their air carriers between the United States, Canada and Europe. Whereas the United States carriers in 1960 enjoyed 50 per cent of the north Atlantic passenger traffic between the United States and Europe, Canada provided only 33 per cent of the scheduled passenger flights between Canada and Europe. This is apart from passenger charter flights where greater imbalance exists. On the north Atlantic routes, there are about 49 foreign

carrier weekly flights compared with 25 Canadian carrier weekly flights. This makes the percentage of weekly flights originating in Canada 33.8.
I submit that although a reasonable balance of flights exists on the Canadian-United Kingdom routes under the Canadian-British pool arrangement, this balance is completely destroyed by the fact that the passenger fare from western Canada to the United Kingdom through the New York gateway via Toronto is identical to that from western Canada to the United Kingdom through Montreal under the pool. I suggest then that the pool can be, and is being, circumvented by way of New York to an alarming extent. I point out that while the Canadian passenger may choose between 22 Canadian and 23 British flights per week under the pool arrangement, he has 45 additional British flights per week to choose from via Toronto-New York at the same price.
The above advantage to the British carrier is tunneling Canadian passengers to the United Kingdom through New York. This advantage is also enjoyed by Air France, K.L.M. and Lufthansa to continental Europe. These foreign carriers maintain large sales offices in every major Canadian city. The figure of 33.8 per cent of the north Atlantic schedule air service from Canada now provided by Canadian carriers is being vastly diluted by the great number of weekly flights available through New York at the same price.

found in the north Atlantic air freight service. At the present time no Canadian carrier operates an all-cargo service over the north Atlantic. Total cargo carried over this route increased by 33.7 per cent-United States carriers included-during 1960. Total cargo carried in 1960 between Canada and Europe was 4,664.6 tons. The share of this amount carried by Canadian air lines in the holds of passenger flights was 1,518.6 tons. This amounts to 32 per cent of the total cargo carried to and from Canada and Europe. Scheduled cargo flights from Canada to Europe planned for 1961 are as follows: K.L.M., six weekly; B.O.A.C., two weekly; C.P.A., nil; T.C.A., nil. B.O.A.C. have two DC-7's converted to freighters and are converting two more. Canadian carriers have similar aircraft which are suitable for cargo conversion. In Canada we also have the best cargo aircraft in the world, designed specifically for air freight, namely the CL-44. To date, no Canadian carrier has given any indication of interest in this national achievement.
Another unfavourable imbalance in Can-ada-Caribbean scheduled passenger service is reflected in the following comparison. Eleven weekly flights are scheduled by foreign air lines from Montreal to Bermuda while only five are scheduled from Montreal and Toronto by Canadian air lines.
May I touch on the Pacific-Orient schedule passenger service. It is also important to point out that the main source of imbalance in this area exists because the Canadian carrier does not have United Kingdom landing rights on its Vancouver-transpolar-Europe route; the contention being that the greatest passenger revenue source lies between Australia, New Zealand, Hong Kong and the United Kingdom. Qantas, on the other hand, enjoys Orient-San Francisco-New York-London rights with pickup rates between Vancouver and San Francisco. This places the Canadian carrier at a distinct competitive disadvantage.
The Canadian air lines pilots' association asserted, on the basis of many years of active association and participation in the Canadian aviation industry, that foreign carriers are getting far more than their share of the air passenger and freight service from this country. I am glad to present its suggestions designed with the sincere hope of giving some assistance to the minister in his consideration of this problem.
The following quotation has a point: "A recession is greatly a state of mind". This point is made in requesting a vigorous nationally sponsored campaign to encourage Canadian passengers and shippers to patronize their own air lines. Some non-members of A.I.T.A., and even some members of A.I.T.A., extend

Supply-Transport
special discounts to their own nationals. It is recommended that special discounts be granted to Canadian citizens by Canadian carriers in order to discourage the equal-fare drain of Canadian business to such gateways as New York-to-Europe and the Caribbean.
Extension consideration must also be given to air cargo. It is well known that the majority of stock in the major Canadian carriers is held by the Canadian railways. Consequently, it is understandable that considerable reserve will necessarily dominate any decision by these air lines to enter actively into the air freight markets to the detriment of their major stockholders. It is respectfully submitted, however, that it is this very prejudice that is allowing foreign air freighters to carry approximately 68 per cent of the Canadian cargo and mail across the north Atlantic.
While considerable air freight is being carried into and across the Canadian Arctic, this service is conducted in its entirety with completely antiquated, obsolete and often dilapidated air freighters of quarter century vintage, while the very best freighter in the world, the swing-tailed CL-44, very desperately awaits adequate orders at its factory at Montreal.
Consideration must be given to the equipment and reequipment of international and external Canadian carriers with the CL-44 with the objective of regenerating the Canadian air freight industry and stimulating the Canadian aircraft industry. The thought is respectfully offered that, while such action might have to be supported by government loans, it might also reduce the annual deficit now being borne by the government, through the capture of this country's rightful share of the world-wide cargo market.
It must be pointed out that while our two major Canadian air lines have been fighting one against the other under what is known as fair trade competition and that the respective mouthpieces of those companies have virtually managed their personal grievances rather than managed their air lines, great consideration should be given to affiliation of our Canadian air carriers.
It is respectfully suggested that an operational and economic affiliation between the major Canadian carriers would be far more beneficial to the Canadian economy than the pool agreement between a Canadian carrier and B.O.A.C. The Canadian carriers cannot afford the luxury of abrasiveness between themselves.
I submit that such Canadian operational and economic affiliation, as compared with Ca-nadian-British affiliation, would so dovetail their routes as to offset seasonal revenue fluctuations with north-south routes against east-west routes. It is felt that only benefit

could come from such an amalgamation not only to the carriers but to the Canadian economy as well.
I also submit that the existence of one-sided foreign service into and through Canadian cities as I have outlined earlier should not be tolerated by our country in that it can only contribute to the stagnation of the Canadian aircraft industry and air line industry and at the same time injure our economy. The government should apply vigorous pressure to equalize those areas where the Canadian industry is not enjoying a fair share of its own market, as I have mentioned earlier.
It is my contention that the major Canadian air lines in conjunction with the Canadian government during the years immediately following world war II were not sufficiently aggressive in carrying the Canadian flag to all parts of the world. I point specifically to K.L.M., S.A.S., Air France, Lufthansa, Sabena and even B.O.A.C. as national flag carriers of countries which were decimated by the war but which have nevertheless subsequently extended their air routes to every corner of the earth. Furthermore, I feel that great effort should be directed toward the acquisition of new routes for the major flag carriers of the Canadian air line industry.
Those responsible for the lagging of this once proud and vigorous industry, which put Canada on the air map at the very beginning of aviation and much earlier than most of our competitors of today, those responsible, as I said, for the present deficit of our two major air lines should take a new look at the possibilities of improving their companies' business through the information given them by the Minister of Transport and the Canadian air lines pilots' association rather than ageing through their personal feud. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I want to turn to a topic on which we have already had some information relating to the announcement as to shipbuilding, and I should like to place some questions and points before the minister. In his announcement as released yesterday the-relevant paragraph on which I wish to touch reads as follows:
However, at a very rough estimate I would expect this should cover between 7,000 and 10,000 man years of additional employment in each year for the next few years in our shipyards-
I am not concerned now with the equal amount of employment in other industries to which he referred. I just want to look at his statement and come back to the inability of the minister and his officials to forecast with any accuracy what the program will amount to in terms of expenditure and employment, I wonder whether the minister's officials have

looked at the statistics of the shipbuilding industry as revealed in the d.b.s. publication of that name. If the minister will take the year 1959 he will see that the statistics for that year in the shipbuilding industry show that there were some 14,000 workers, that salaries and wages totalled $62 million and that the gross value of the products turned out by these 14,000 employees was approximately $143 million.
If the minister could make a calculation of between 7,000 and 10,000 jobs, which is a very appealing figure, I cannot understand why he could not take the average wage as revealed in these statistics and arrive at the expenditure. There is a remarkable comparison all the way through. According to my rough division, the average wage or salary in the shipbuilding industry is around $4,100 a year. If you are providing 10,000 jobs this means a wage bill of approximately $41 million. If the wage bill in the shipbuilding industry in the past has been on the average approximately 45 per cent of the total gross value of the product as it comes out of the yards, this would indicate to me that the estimate of value is going to come out of this announcement, when you correlate the manpower figures with these figures, is somewhere between $75 million and $85 million, and 40 per cent of that at least in the next two years until 1963 cuts you back roughly to a subsidy on the capital cost of somewhere between $30 million and $40 million.
That is a sum immense enough and yet within frontiers that are understandable enough that we fail to see why the minister cannot give us something better than the dollar item that is going to appear in the supplementary estimates. If he can calculate this attractive figure of 7,000 to 10,000 jobs a year, it seems to me that he can take the average figures in the shipbuilding industry because, Lord knows, in an industry where you have unions you are not going to have any great changes either up or down in this pattern. There is a remarkable failure to provide us with a calculation and to provide the country with some estimate, like the job estimate, of what this program is going to cost.
I do not think we will quarrel with an estimated cost of between $30 million and $40 million with respect to the subsidization of the capital cost of shipping. We are not going to do that, but we think that for general financial purposes that is the figure that should be revealed to us and that is the kind of appropriation that should be set aside rather than this dollar item which just throws it wide open. I think we deserve an explanation from the minister as to why he
Supply-Transport
would not push his estimate of the jobs into an estimate of the actual money that the program is going to cost.
There are two other aspects of the shipbuilding announcement on which we need some explanation, and I say this not in criticism but for understanding. One is the matter of Canadian content and how that is going to be written into the question of capital cost. I would assume that the Canadian maritime commission is going to be the body that will determine the capital cost of these vessels, and I am wondering whether it is going to continue under its previous instructions in relation to Canadian content and the encouragement of the use of Canadian machines and equipment within the ships.
The other point on which we deserve an explanation, since there is going to be nothing statutory in relation to this matter is the effect that the minister contemplates this program will have upon the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act. The hon. member for Laurier mentioned this point. While this act, as most members will recall, is complicated in its application, it simply amounts to . giving accelerated depreciation to firms for building ships in Canada. This is a considerable concession although apparently it has not been enough. We would like some estimate from the minister of what is involved for the Department of Finance or the Department of National Revenue so far as this act is concerned with relation to the new subsidy that is going into this field.
If we could have information on these matters during this debate on the estimates of the minister, we would feel much happier about the efficacy of this announcement. My colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East, has suggested that he feels this legislation is related to the by-election in Esqui-malt-Saanich. I will go him one further. I think it may be related to a much bigger election foray. I have no particular quarrel with that but if we are going to have this as a preliminary to tub thumping on the hustings I think we should have more information as to the cost and the application and as there is to be no statutory change I think the minister should give it to us now. We would especially like from him at this time the views of the Department of Finance in this particular matter, and I would ask him this question. Is it possible that the whole matter of what this program may cost will be revealed to us by the Minister of Finance when he brings down his budget?
To reiterate one part of my argument, I say that when you look at the d.b.s. statistics on the shipbuilding industry you see a remarkable stability in the correlation between

employees, wages and gross value of the product. I should like to say how happy I am to congratulate the Minister of Transport upon his assumption of this important and very difficult portfolio. I have had the pleasure of knowing the minister for a long time, a good deal longer I would hazard than has the hon. member for Port Arthur, and I have admired him, and admired the things for which he stood. I am heartily enthusiastic about the great leadership he is giving in this difficult portfolio which means so much to the area which I represent. I suppose there is no minister in the cabinet who receives more letters from me, and I suppose from many of the maritime members, than does the Minister of Transport. In spite of the multitudinous problems we bring to him, he greets us with the courtesy which has always marked his relationships with other people.
We islanders live near the sea and many of us live oft the products of the sea in an economic way, so transportation is of tremendous importance to us. One of the most important problems in the whole Atlantic area is this question of transportation. One of the drawbacks under which we have laboured for many years has been the inadequacy of transportation so we are, therefore, extremely

interested in the type of minister who is in charge of this department. There are many items in the province of Prince Edward Island alone which are of importance to our economic life and upon which the actions and decisions of the government through this Department of Transport have a major bearing. Not long ago in the city of Charlottetown a new 7,000-foot runway was opened. This has meant a great deal to that community and to our province. Had this runway not been constructed, the very fine industry established by Enamel and Heating Products Limited would not have been possible. This new runway was sought by the city of Charlottetown for many years, and for many years it was refused.
We are pleased, too, with the developments in the marine service which have recently taken place. I thought it was very appropriate that the department's new boat based at Charlottetown, for the Charlottetown marine disrict, should be called the Tupper. Tupper was one of the fathers of confederation who performed so magnificently nearly a hundred years ago when he came to the Charlottetown conference, at which conference it has been said he formed an offensive and defensive alliance with Sir John A. Macdonald as he later came to be. I am pleased, too, that the department has authorized the construction of an additional ferry. I refer to the one which is under construction at Halifax, although little progress has been made on this vessel lately because of labour difficulties.
I was pleased this morning to hear the minister's reference to the extension of new facilities to the docks at Borden. He mentioned an impressive figure of $980,000. Recently we have seen his interest in the field of subsidies as indicated by the grant of a new subsidy to the important service between Prince Edward Island and the north shore of the St. Lawrence. This will be very helpful to our primary producers and will act as a stimulant to our whole economy. We have discovered in the maritimes that the development of the St. Lawrence seaway brings new prospects for trade with the area at the mouth of the St. Lawrence. Prince Edward Island, with its surplus of fine agricultural products, is ideally suited for trade with the north shore ports.
In this connection, I should like to say a word about the new chairman of the maritime commission. He is a man, it seems to me, who understands the situation and has been most co-operative and most perceptive in looking at the needs of the Atlantic community. I should like to mention one more item to complete my complimentary list before I commence making suggestions to the minister. I

want to mention the establishment of direct T.C.A. service to Halifax. With all due respect to other parts of Canada, I always thought it highly unfortunate that so many of our visitors from Europe made their first contact with Canada at Montreal. They then went across Canada and missed seeing the Atlantic provinces. No one could possibly know much about Canada with such a neglectful approach as that. It is possible now to land directly at Halifax and then start the journey in the Atlantic provinces where it should commence.
Mr. Chairman, in a previous session of parliament I used as a paper, one might say, the timetable of the Canadian National Railways. I was not asked to table the document because it is fairly well known. I was impressed then, as I am impressed now though still not favourably, by the comparison between the service provided by the Canadian National between Montreal and Ottawa, a distance of 116.1 miles, and the service provided between the city of Charlottetown and the city of Moncton, a distance of 126.8 miles. You leave Moncton at 2.40 and you arrive at Charlottetown at nine o'clock. When you leave Ottawa at 3.30, you get to Montreal at 5.30 o'clock. The difference is phenomenal. I would ask the minister to use his influence with Canadian National Railways to correct this situation as they seek to gain for themselves a greater share of the traffic. We all know the difficulties under which the railways are operating at this time. One of the keynotes in any program to attract a greater share of the traffic is good service. The kind of service I have mentioned to the capital of Prince Edward Island is not good enough. There is no reason why we should spend so many hours travelling from Moncton to Charlottetown. There may be slower runs in some parts of the country, but I am not familiar with many that would compare so uncomfortably.
We islanders never ask for too much and our suggestions are always moderate and modest, but there is one more item that might be brought to the attention of the minister. In addition to the old, familiar lifeline formed by the car ferry that runs between Tormen-tine and Borden, there has been established a new ferry between Wood Islands and Caribou, the latter point in the constituency of my good friend, the member for Pictou. The traffic increase on this run has been rapid in recent years. We have a very fine snipe appropriately named the Lord Selkirk which handles the traffic well and makes the run in proper time. Automobiles are moved on and off quickly with that new boat. There is also a fairly ancient ship which has a fine record and does its best but it cannot by any means cope with the demands of the

traffic. Just as soon as possible-and we were talking about shipbuilding a while ago in this committee-I think efforts should be made to bring along either a sister ship to the Lord Selkirk or one as modern, effective and efficient. If that is done, it will look after, for some time, this section between Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.
I suppose no minister of transport would ever expect any Prince Edward Island member of parliament to discuss his estimates without making some mention of the ferry service between Borden and Tormentine. Indeed, if one went back over Hansard covering the debates of this house since Prince Edward Island entered confederation in 1873, he would find that was the one thread of consistency. Indeed, it is said that no Prince Edward Island politician ever really gets under way unless he has prepared and delivered one speech on transportation across the straits. If he has ever had any difficulty in getting across there, as have many islanders, he will utter that speech with all the more fervour and sincerity.
This does not come into the category of a request of the government. This comes in the category of consideration of the proper fulfilment of a confederation pledge. Ferry service is always on the minds of islanders because we regard this service-and we cannot help doing so-as an economic lifeline. This year the province of Prince Edward Island has endured the worst winter since 1905. I suppose this fact proves the old adage that the rain falls on the just and on the unjust.
And snow.

There have been many holdups in connection with the crossing of the ferries. Those in charge of the ships have done very well. But when you find the depth, width, extent and continuity of ice that there has been in the Northumberand strait in the last number of months-it seems like six months-the situation can be understood. Of course these matters are beyond the control of the Minister of Transport himself. Nevertheless it has brought into sharper focus than ever the problem with respect to this important ferry. I mentioned earlier the fact that an additional boat is being built at Halifax. This boat will certainly be needed. I would suggest that akin to that but separate from it is the very important consideration of a replacement of at least one of the existing boats. The secondary ferry the Prince Edward Island is a boat that is now older than is the junior member for Queens. When Robert Borden came to Charlottetown in 1911 -I was not there but I acquired this information through going back through the history-he said to the people of the island, "You

have been wanting a car ferry. Elect me as prime minister of Canada and you will get one". They did and he did. However, the same boat is still there doing valiant service. As much as we love Sir Robert Borden in Prince Edward Island and as much as we prize that old ship-it certainly was a credit to the builders-we would think that an urgent move to replace the Prince Edward Island would be very much in order.
The estimates of the Minister of Transport are before us, not those of the Minister of Public Works. If this latter were the ease, I would be discussing the causeway. However, it is difficult to dissociate completely the two subjects. If the causeway should be proven not feasible, it would be up to the Minister of Transport, as the dominion minister responsible for overseeing this confederation pledge, to give us continuous and efficient communication with the mainland and it would be his responsibility to start a process whereby we would have the most up-to-date ferry service possible.

some very good ammunition which I know the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will support me in using, when the time comes.

If, however, the causeway is judged feasible, and if it is undertaken very soon indeed, it cannot be completed before the Prince Edward Island boat aforesaid is too old for the service. Therefore, the minister will still be faced with the situation of providing yet another boat. 1 started off by saying that we are modest people, but I see no other solution to the situation except the provision of yet another boat.
No doubt the experts in the Department of Transport have looked at the figures with reference to travel by people from other parts of Canada, from the United States and indeed from other continents to Prince Edward Island. Back in 1943 fewer than 10,000 automobiles were carried across the strait. In 1947 the figure rose to 27,000 and in 1960 the figure was 171,500. I need hardly say that this is a growing service. I need hardly underscore the need for providing increased facilities. Last summer in the midst of the demand, I should say through you, Mr. Chairman, to the minister, the most elaborate facilities were provided in the trans-strait service. More boats were making more trips than ever before, and I am happy to say that the service was enthusiastically applauded by those who undertook it. As I mentioned with respect to the estimates of another department not so long ago, we had more tourists last year than ever before and it is likely their numbers will continue to increase, because once people come to Prince Edward Island they will return and tell their friends what a wonderful place it is.
We are counting on the Minister of Transport to see that our service will be so good that even if-God forbid-we have another winter as tough as this one, or as tough as the winter of '05 which I do not personally remember, we shall be able to get through the wind, ice, sleet and snow, and that he, like Robert Borden will update the transportation facilities and give us the finest and best type of transportation to the mainland we have ever had.
I wish I had time to say more, but I have given my usual undertaking to be brief. I should only say this. At times I have been a little disturbed that, perhaps, as a result of events which were taking place in Canada, if the party to which I belong should make an appeal to the people it might suffer the loss of one or two seats. However, having heard today the reactions of certain hon. gentlemen

opposite to the minister's splendid announcement regarding shipbuilding, recalling their reaction to the recent announcement made by the Minister of Agriculture concerning our sales of wheat to China, I have assured myself that even those limited fears were utterly groundless.

I am pleased to rise to take part in this debate, and at the outset I wish to express my appreciation of the capable performance of the Minister of Transport since his appointment. The shipping policy which the hon. gentleman announced on Friday is without a doubt the best move that this government could have made toward the creation of job opportunities in the shipbuilding industries. I have personally advocated such a policy ever since my election to parliament in 1958, and I should like to quote a few paragraphs from a speech I delivered in this house on June 27, 1960, as reported at page 5451 of Hansard.
A tew moments ago I was trying to point out the importance of having a Canadian merchant marine. The Canadian great lakes shipping industry could provide the foundation upon which to build an international commercial fleet worthy of a major trading nation. During the war. Canada built training and fighting ships. Some of these were built at the Port Arthur shipbuilding yard which at present is not doing much. However, this yard has the experience in both management and personnel to build ships for any purpose. It is regrettable that many ships of Canadian registry were built in foreign shipyards, and that many more are being built abroad. The federal government could bolster dwindling employment in Canadian shipyards by encouraging shipbuilding in every possible way. We are subsidizing wheat growers, hog producers, egg producers, coal mines, gold mines, and railways; why not give a little help to the shipbuilding industry? Why not reestablish the Canadian merchant marine which was allowed to disappear so ingloriously a couple of years ago? Whatever the circumstances surrounding the disposal of those ships, the action taken at that time has not added to the stature of our nation. If a mistake was made-and I submit that the sale of those eight ships to Cuba was a mistake-let us admit it and renew our efforts with the vigour which is the characteristic of everything Canadian.
I realize that enthusiasm for the idea of a subsidized merchant fleet would probably be challenged on the ground that it would result in additional taxes, but I submit that the benefits resulting from a policy of assistance to shipbuilding and the development of a merchant fleet would more than offset the cost of such a program.
Not long ago I saw a report in a newspaper to the effect that Greece intends to spend more than $10 million to build a fleet of six freighters for the great lakes-Mediterranean trade. This means that the Hellenic lines will be entering the St Lawrence seaway for the first time. These ships will bear cargoes to and from such ports as Naples, Istanbul and Beirut, and they are expected to be put into service by the summer of 1961.
Where will these freighters be built? Not in Canada. Our exports and imports will be carried through the great lakes by vessels of other countries.
Supply-Transport
Canada builds fewer ships than Finland. Our deep-sea fleet, which ten years ago numbered some 200 vessels, is now less than a dozen and these are mainly oil tankers sailing between the United States and Canadian ports.
Our shores front on three great oceans, the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Arctic. I especially want to underline the reference to the Arctic ocean. If the Prime Minister's vision ever comes to fruition and we witness an increased development of the north the Arctic ocean will become a great sea lane. In addition we have the great lakes system which in itself could be classed as another ocean.
Despite all this other nations build ships for us. Other nations operate ships for us. All this is true, because we say we cannot possibly afford to build and operate ships ourselves. Then we wonder why we have so many unemployed. The time has surely come to sound a clarion call for the reconstruction and expansion of a national merchant marine. I commend the suggestion to the minister and to the government. They have the power to initiate a movement to bring back our merchant marine and establish our nation in the forefront of seafaring nations of the world. We are the third largest trading nation of the world but so far as shipping is concerned our position is not much superior to that of Switzerland. I sincerely trust that the government will take action as quickly as possible.
I feel strongly about this, Mr. Chairman, because as Canadians we are often prone to boast of our national resources. We boast about what we have under the ground and above it but we say little about the exploitation of what we have in our own country for the benefit of Canadians and for the benefit of those who will come to our shores in the years ahead. I commend to the government consideration of this great challenge that faces us from coast to coast.
I know that objections will be raised. Some will say that this is all nonsense and that it would cost millions of dollars. It probably would represent a large expenditure but it would be worth it. It would be a Canadian enterprise of which we would be proud and in years to come we could look back upon it as something worth while. Let this 24th parliament take action.
That is the end of the quotation from my speech.
At the Liberal rally held in Ottawa last January, at the meeting of the committee on transport I moved a resolution which met with the approval of that body. I quote that resolution because I wish to have it on the record:
Whereas the greater proportion of world's commerce is still being carried by sea going ships, and
Whereas Canada is the world's third trading nation, but no ships flying the red ensign are ever seen on the sea lanes of the world, and
Whereas ten years ago our deep-sea fleet numbered 200 vessels, now being down to fewer than a dozen, namely oil tankers, and
Whereas our shipbuilding industry is now practically at a standstill with thousands of skilled workers unemployed,
Therefore, be it resolved that a Canadian merchant marine be established, and that a formula of assistance to Canadian shipyards be considered, to stimulate shipbuilding in Canada.
It is only natural, therefore, Mr. Chairman, that I should be pleased with the announcement made by the minister to the effect that Canadian shipowners will be able to obtain

new vessels at reasonable and competitive prices instead of having them built abroad because of lower construction costs. I assume that this will be accomplished with a formula of subsidies which might bring about the gradual creation of a Canadian merchant marine and the beginning of a deep-sea fleet.
Perhaps the government could give some consideration to the establishment of a Canadian coast guard, something which the advent of the St. Lawrence seaway has made not only desirable but necessary. Of course the coasts of the great lakes are not the oniy coasts that need guarding; both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts require patrolling. Coastguard vessels are badly needed and I hope that in this new Canadian marine policy will be included a provision for a Canadian coastguard.
On April 18, 1961 I asked the minister whether he was in a position to indicate to the house if the government intended to bring in legislation which would eliminate unfair competition from commonwealth registered ships which are now permitted to carry goods between Canadian ports. The reply is found in Hansard for that date at page 3747 and reads as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I am looking into the matter at the present time. Further examination by my department is necessary. As I indicated previously, I expect to have something to say about shipping policy generally before this session ends.
The announcement has been made that consideration has been given to these problems affecting the great lakes areas due to the commonwealth shipping agreement under which vessels of commonwealth registry are enabled to engage in domestic coastal trade. The government is evidently conscious of the unfair competition of these ships of commonwealth registry, which is adversely affecting Canadian ships. All in all, the announcement should be welcomed by most Canadians.
I should also like to say a word about the seaway which is now beginning its third year of operations. Ocean-going vessels are now seen on the seaway from Montreal to the Canadian lakehead, and with the enlargement of the Welland canal, the effects are more clearly seen, and ever increasing traffic can be safely predicted.
As an example, the total overseas imports into both Canada and the United States, through the St. Lawrence section of the seaway increased 400 per cent since 1958; a gain from 500,000 tons to 2.1 million tons in 1960. Seaway borne exports expanded even more in 1960, amounting to 5.3 million tons, nearly 10 times the 1958 figure.

Overseas exports of wheat carried directly from the lakehead ports of Fort William and Port Arthur which, before the opening of the seaway, was only a small amount, now accounts for nearly 5 per cent of Canada's total wheat exports. It has been reported that 750 ships will be required to carry the wheat which was sold recently to China. I wonder whether it would not be as economical to move some of this wheat through the lakehead ports and around the Panama canal. Of course, this may not be a practical idea, but it could save on the cost of shipment by rail from Manitoba and Saskatchewan to the Pacific coast.
With all its growing pains and difficulties encountered, especially during the first two years of operation, we can safely say that this gigantic enterprise has certainly proved its worth, and that it will be, and is, a great monument to those who conceived the idea, and those who made the decisions to proceed with the project.
On March 2 of this year the minister addressed the annual meeting of the Fort William chamber of commerce, and he devoted a major portion of his speech to air transport.
There is no question that the airport which serves Fort William, Port Arthur and district, has developed to the point where it requires extensive expansion if it is to meet the continuing increase in demand for air transportation, which has indeed become an almost integral part of our business life today.
The minister at one point in his address said that an estimated $110,000 will be spent this year toward improvement of the airport, and also that plans have been made for an extension of the air terminal building, to triple its capacity to handle travellers. This, together with several other improvements will bring the total expenditures for these expansions and renovations to $650,000.
He also made the statement, with which we cannot quarrel, that, where airport accommodation is concerned, the department is endeavouring to concentrate its plans on needs for the next ten years. This is a sensible approach to the question of meeting the needs of that growing army of air travellers which make Mr. R. G. McGregor's heart beat with warm anticipation and pleasure.
The people of Fort William were pleased to hear the minister paint such a glowing picture of progress for the future of the lake-head in terms of air and sea transportation, and I hope that he will tell us how soon we may expect action on this program of expansion at the lakehead airport.
The advent of fast jet airliners has not improved Trans-Canada Air Lines service to the lakehead. These jets do not stop there, with the result that we now only have two two-way

flights connecting the lakehead with Toronto and Ottawa. I wonder whether there could be some way of improving this service.
And now I wish to deal briefly with perhaps the greatest medium of transportation which made confederation possible in 1867, namely our railways. We can go back to our first prime ministers, Sir John A. Macdonald, Scottish born, and the French Canadian, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. These two great prime ministers were the embodiment of what was the best of the two great historical parties, the parties which will continue to give Canada good government, we hope, and a government of free enterprise without distinction of class. Both these prime ministers strongly supported the first trans-continental railway system as being the only link binding together all parts of Canada and thus forming this young, vigorous nation. They stood shoulder to shoulder in advocating low cost transportation to promote the spread of our population and the development of our resources.
Here I wish to quote Sir Wilfrid Laurier speaking in parliament in support of the railways:
To provide immediate means whereby the products of the new settlers may find an exit to the ocean at the least possible cost and whereby likewise a market may be found in our new regions for those who toil in the forests, in the mines and in the shops of the older provinces. Such is our duty, it is immediate and imperative. Heaven grant that it be not already too late.
At that time a policy was implemented under which shippers were charged on the basis of their ability to pay-in other words, low cost freight rates-and here subsidization was born. Succeeding governments have been more or less, and with very little variation, carrying on a method of subsidization to meet increasing operating costs, the latest being the $97 million for 1961, of which the Canadian National Railways will receive $57 million and a fraction and the Canadian Pacific Railway $39 million and a fraction. According to the recommendation of the royal commission on transportation, the annual amount is to be scaled down until at the end of five years the total will be reduced to $47 million for the two railways. These annual subsidies are the cause of considerable alarm and criticism against the two great trans-continental systems. However, it should not be forgotten that the Canadian National Railways, for example, is made up of a group of private railroads which went bankrupt many years ago. It has been an instrument of the government in opening up the country in which it is still being used.
In dealing with the first report of the royal commission I wish to point out that 90205-6-303i
