the commission substantially agrees with the submission of the lakehead cities to the commission to the effect that horizontal increases on a percentage basis cause unfair distribution of the freight rate burden; also, that freight rates, including increases which the carriers cannot collect, are unrealistic and impose an unfair burden on the so-called "captive traffic" forced to use the rails and to assume the maximum cost; also that certain losses in the passenger service which fares cannot cover should not be a charge on the freight rate structure. While subsidies, which of course nobody likes, are seemingly necessary as the only means of helping the present situation, the carriers should use every possible means to reduce the need for this assistance.
On page 34 of the commission report I find the following:
All industries and regions feel that their particular transportation problems are great and important. It is too much to ask from a rail user in Newfoundland, at the lakehead, or in the Okanagan valley that he agree that the difficulties he has brought before the commission are of a lesser significance than, for instance, the problems of the maritime provinces. How true; and to get the full benefit of this statement one must know how highly the maritimes have rated the importance of the maritimes, with some justification, all down through the years.
This quotation seems to bear out our contention that northwestern Ontario has been penalized with a discriminatory set of freight rates which have militated against a greater expansion of trade and industry at the lake-head.
These are the few suggestions I have presented to the minister here this afternoon. I trust they will be given some consideration. As a matter of fact, they deserve deep study. They require some expert opinion. They require the experts of the department to go into them fully and to see whether or not any of them have merit. I am of the belief that they have merit, and that it will help Canada greatly if the suggestions are implemented.
Before the end of the discussions of these estimates I hope the minister will be able to give us the answers to many of the questions which have been asked and that he will be in a position to come forward with something which we shall all be pleased to hear.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few moments of the committee's time to discuss the minister's estimates from the point of view of the development of the north country. Before passing to the main theme of my remarks, which will be criticism of the present policy of the issuance of class C and B licences in air transportation in the north, I should like to draw the

Supply-Transport
minister's attention to a number of problems that come under the jurisdiction of his department in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. Many of those have been solved in the last two or three years, and many point up very dramatically the difference between the activities of the department in the northern part of our country now as compared with the lack of such activities in the past.
Before informing the members of the committee on those points, I should like to take issue with one of the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat when he described the support which Sir Wilfrid Laurier gave to the building of the railroad at that time. He forgets, I am sure, the expression coined by the Liberal opponents of the transcontinental railroad of that day about building a railroad from wigwam to wigwam. It seems to me that a similar expression was used by their present leader in recent years. I cannot refrain from reverting to the discussion of the other day with the Leader of the Opposition about his statement concerning the building of roads from igloo to igloo.
In the last two years the department has been responsible for a great expansion of communications generally in the north. In the Yukon and Northwest Territories telephone facilities have been installed where they were not available before. A new line has been constructed from Whitehorse through to Mayo, Dawson City and Elsa as well as new lines in the Northwest Territories. This has made it possible for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to provide services to this part of the country where none existed before apart from one or two voluntarily operated stations in the larger communities.
The department has been improving the airport and navigational facilities at the larger airports in the north in a very commendable fashion. The activities of the department have resulted generally in a raising of the standards of air transport in the north and this in turn has provided a certain stimulus to travel to these northern regions. However, there is still much to be done. I might draw the minister's attention to the need for extending the runway at Dawson City. With the Klondike festival targeted for 1962, it is very necessary that this airport be extended to the point where it is able to handle four-engine aircraft. There will be a larger number of tourists who will wish to travel to Dawson City for this event and it will be found that a good deal of this traffic will not be realized unless four-engine aircraft are provided with facilities at Dawson City.
Mayo airport is also due for enlargement to handle four-engine aircraft. This airport is right in the heart of a highly mineralized

area. United Keno Hill mine operating in this area now provides with its one silver mine almost as much in dollar revenue to the Canadian economy as the 20 silver mines of British Columbia and the 12 silver mines of Ontario. Therefore improved facilities at this point are very essential.
I would also draw the minister's attention to the departmental plans concerning the improvement of facilities at the Whitehorse airport. I understand that plans exist for the conversion of one of the existing hangars at the Whitehorse airport in order to provide larger terminal facilities. With the traffic in and out of Whitehorse, which is the main centre on what was known at one time as the northwest stageing route, the facilities required here are not so extensive that the minister could not, I am sure, obtain co-operation from the other government departments requiring space therein.
There is another point I should like to draw to the minister's attention, the maintenance of emergency strips in the north generally. Emergency air strips are very essential in facilitating air traffic and air safety in the north and in my belief much more can be done to improve these very necessary facilities.
One point about which I am particularly concerned has to do with the large turnover in meteorological workers in the northern areas although I believe the problem is national. In these scientific workers we have some of the most highly skilled individuals on the government payroll and yet they are one of the worst paid groups of scientists. These people must have university educations before they undertake their duties and unless much more attention is given to establishing a proper wage structure for meteorologists in the service of the Department of Transport I believe the minister and the department will continue to be faced with difficulties in replacing a large number of these employees who seek employment in the United States and elsewhere where wages are much more attractive.
Specifically, Mr. Chairman, I want to deal with the government's policy in connection with the granting of licences for the operation of non-scheduled commercial air services. In December of 1959 the then minister, who is now Minister of Trade and Commerce, announced that a more liberal policy was being implemented with regard to applications for licences for non-scheduled commercial air services involving small light aircraft and helicopters. It had been decided that, except in unusual circumstances, applications for air services in these categories would not be refused on the grounds of protection of existing operators or restriction of

competition but rather would be made available on a liberal basis in accordance with the spirit of free enterprise.
Prior to the announcement of that policy the principle upon which air transport licences had been granted to non-scheduled commercial air services was based on the need for protecting charter operators out of bases in all areas of Canada so that a healthy and high quality growth in the service concerned would be encouraged. I am not aware how the new policy is working out in the rest of Canada but I can assure the minister it is not having the desired effect in the north. The air transport board now, in exercising its licensing function under the Aeronautics Act, is granting a larger number of class C and class B licences. If the policy is continued I believe that the previous high standard of services provided by these charter operators in the north is going to deteriorate substantially particularly with regard to the operation of helicopters. In January of 1960 the air industries and transport association of Canada submitted a brief to the Prime Minister wherein they set forth their views, and I wish to quote briefly from their submission as follows:
Notwithstanding our submission the Minister of Transport, on December 18, announced the policy of decontrolling non-scheduled air services as defined by the air transport board as being in group "B".
It is therefore our opinion in the light of our earlier submission that we would be remiss in not advising you of the very serious implications of this policy.
While Canada can be justly proud in having recently celebrated its fiftieth anniversary of powered flight, it was not until the thirties that aviation started to show its potential importance to the development of the north. From that period to the year 1945 air carriers operated without any regulatory control for the benefit of the public necessity, convenience or interest. It is a well known fact that this lack of control had a devastating effect on the growth of this industry ...
The potential is only so great and unlimited competition is not the answer.
I should like now to draw the minister's attention to the operations of Eldorado Aviation Limited, a subsidiary of Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, a crown corporation, and also since it comes under the jurisdiction of the department, the operations of Northern Transportation Company Limited, a water carrier on the Mackenzie river system. In my view, the services of these two subsidiaries have outlived their usefulness, and there should not be a continuation of government subsidies to these organizations in direct competition with the private carriers in the north. Pacific Western Airlines, who now operate services up and down the Mackenzie system from Edmonton and other northern provincial points, is in trouble because of declining load factor which could easily be improved by
Supply-Transport
the amount of traffic carried by Eldorado Aviation Limited. P.W.A. is operating a high quality service in the northern regions and is operating on a high standard of safety. This, of course, will continue. There is no doubt, however, that P.W.A. will have to diminish the service it is now supplying to these areas if the operations of Eldorado Aviation Limited are allowed to continue to eat into the potential traffic. For instance, over 8,000 passengers were carried by this crown subsidized corporation during 1960.
Two of the conclusions reached by the air industries and transport association are, one, that the situation will not only stifle but submerge a young and growing industry-that is what it is-which has been one of the major factors in the opening up of Canada's north. Second, the continued implementation of such a liberal policy will result in a situation which could have a vital bearing on the safety of travel and, more specifically, to Canada's north with the obvious resultant expense to search and rescue.
The air carrier, Mr. Chairman, has been for some years basically the prime instrument in the development of the north. The system under which the operator has been able to produce and exist is based on a minimum of protection. In return, he establishes permanent facilities and, as such, becomes a permanent part of the community he serves. It should be pointed out these facilities are provided at the expense of the operators. The Air Industries and Transport Association of Canada is not the only group that is concerned with air development in northern Canada. There are several other organizations, but I do not wish to take up the time of the committee by quoting extensively from correspondence I have had with these other associations.
I should like to put it to the minister that there are a number of ways in which the development of air services in northern areas could be helped. I am constrained to say, however, that they amount to a subsidy of some sort. I am sure that in the transportation field, however, subsidies are not a strange animal to the government. I should like to enumerate some of these ways. A direct operating subsidy could be given to the air lines involved in these northern regions. Second, a fuel rebate could be granted on fuel boarded in the north which would equate the cost of fuel to these northern operators with the cost of fuel in urban areas. Fuel cost is a major air line operating expense, and the saving to the air lines could be passed on to the customers. The exploration of other benefits could probably reveal other

Supply-Transport
ways of equating northern operating costs with those of the more economical intercity services.
Another major air line expense is the cost of equipment. The government could underwrite part of the cost of the airplanes in order to make it easier for the air lines to equip or to re-equip. This form of subsidy is used in connection with the civil air reserve plan in the United States. The policy there is that it is in the national interest to further increase the number of individual aircraft available to handle any national emergency. The aircraft purchased by air lines for profit will not provide this capacity because profit margins require high load factors and, therefore, the government will help with the equipment bill if the result provides more aircraft than would have been purchased otherwise.
There are, however, some restrictions imposed. The air lines must agree to release part of their fleet to the nation when required and must buy a type of aircraft which can be used as military transport. I think Canada has taken a most dramatic lead here with the development of the de Havilland Caribou. A plan similar to that which has been devised in the United States would certainly help all aviation in this country.
Another factor in considering this problem is the used aircraft market. This is no longer good and has not been for some time because of the rapid technological developments in this field. Depreciation will become a problem for air lines, and it is a problem for some of the smaller operators now. The government could maintain a market for used aircraft at good prices, thereby encouraging their replacement. This would benefit the country as well as the air lines, in that it would help keep the aircraft modern. The new aircraft are better in every way, including economy of operation.
Another field to which I have devoted some thought is the operation of the R.C.A.F. transport command. I think this could be redefined. The R.C.A.F. now does a lot of northern transport flying which could be handled by commercial operators. Many people believe that the R.C.A.F. should be limited in transport operations to operational support transport and that air lines should be integrated into the defence picture in a way similar to the merchant marine. This is an involved suggestion, but a plan which offers civilians peacetime use from defence expenditures is certainly worth considering. It can be pointed out, too, that an expanded civil air fleet would provide some jobs for the many fine pilots trained by the R.C.A.F. who now, on discharge, find it almost impossible to practise their chosen vocation.

The government could benefit northern air transport greatly if some money were spent on facilities. Northern airports, navigation aids, alternate airports, instrument approach facilities, and night flying facilities need a great deal of improvement. This is true, in spite of the rapid strides the government has been making in improving these facilities. At some stages the air lines own and operate essential equipment themselves. This imposes an additional and unnecessary cost on their operations, which cost is reflected in their service. A lot of present day flying in the north is contract supply to D.E.W. line bases. I think it could be considered that these bases will remain in operation for some time and that a permanent air transport service is warranted. The present system of annual contracts does not encourage the kind of air line growth which has any real benefit to the country. I refer to the fact that these supply contracts are renegotiated annually.
I am not suggesting for a moment that the government, through T.C.A. or any other government service, should go into the north and compete with air lines now operating in the north. On the few northern runs these private companies have left, there is hardly enough to support the service they now provide. As a matter of fact P.W.A. in the Mackenzie system has not enough traffic to support the service they are now operating.
As I have already pointed out, air transport is like all other transportation. It is a matter that is vital to the country, affecting its growth, its prosperity and its defence. The government should appreciate these factors and give careful attention to the development of policies which will be consistent therewith. If we have earned any special criticism in so far as our air line policy is concerned, I think it is because it has not been definitive enough; whereas in the past administration there was absolutely no really definitive policy in so far as the development of air line transport in this country is concerned or, if there was a policy, it was a policy of reaction, laissez-faire, or "We will do something when something appears on the horizon". From this we have advanced at least to the point where we can discern certain definitive avenues in our air transport policies. But these are not yet cohesive and they still must be evolved into a plan which will insure the realization of the factors of growth, prosperity and defence, as I have pointed out. The government as yet has not involved itself deeply in this problem, in my view, and I feel that the time is far past when we should have done so. These are the remarks I have to make concerning the development of air transport particularly relating to the north and I confide them to the minister in the

hope that they will, to use a phrase that I have learned from both sides of the chamber, get the consideration they deserve.

In connection with the
minister's announcement, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I am very much in favour of helping our shipbuilding industry. I also hope that our Canadian trade between Canadian ports will be carried by Canadian ships and will thus increase employment. I do not believe this matter of helping the shipbuilding industry should be handled by way of a vote of $1 in the estimates. I am in favour of helping the industry in a proper manner. The government should give us an estimate and we could vote it. I think the government should be able to give that estimate and if they did not have enough money, they could come back for more and we would gladly vote it here in this chamber. I do not think any hon. member would be opposed to it. This whole thing seems to be trickery on the part of the government. The Minister of Finance will show $1 as an expenditure, and although expenditures can go up to $40 million, $50 million or even $100 million and they will just show as $1. At the present time we know that his books are away out of balance and that he wants to avoid putting extra expenditures in his budget. He is just going to put in $1 and it will not even stand that.
Pre-election procedure.
That is right.

To me this is taking away the rights of parliament, to show just a $1 expenditure and be able to go ahead and spend millions. Where are the rights of parliament? What about the bill of rights? We have not so many rights left. If this was a bill, we could refer it to the Minister of Justice and he would pass his opinion on it. However, it is not a bill, and we therefore cannot get his opinion on whether or not this might come within the bill of rights or whether we are leaving with parliament the right to vote money.
Business of the House
I want to deal with something particular, Mr. Chairman. It has to do with a matter in my own area. Since it will probably take me 10 minutes to deal with it and as it is nearly six o'clock now, may I call it six o'clock.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
1.	In the fiscal year ended March 31, 1960, what were the total expenditures of the government of Canada in the interest of civil defence?
2.	What was the estimated cost of expenditures for this period on the part of the provincial governments?
3.	What is the estimated cost of expenditures in this regard during the same period on the part of municipal governments?
4.	What is the estimated total cost of expenditures by all levels of government for the fiscal period mentioned above?
5.	What consideration has been given by the government to the project of changing the name from "civil defence" to "civil disaster"?
6.	Has the government any record of the number of homes that have built basement shelters? If so, how many have been built?
7.	What recommendation in this regard has the government to make to people living in apartments in concentrated urban areas?
8.	How much money has already been spent on the proposed project of moving the seat of effective government out of Ottawa in case of a nuclear war?
9.	Who has been designated to decide as to who will be eligible for priority in the proposed movement of government authority out of Ottawa in case of a nuclear war?
10.	Who is on the priority list referred to in the above question?
Answer by: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker
(Prime Minister):
1.	Apart from army expenditure on survival operations and communications, where the expenditures in aid of civil defence and continuity of government cannot be accurately segregated, the total expenditures on civil defence measures and other preparations for civilian measures to be taken in wartime were $4,635,832.
2.	$574,903, excluding those reimbursed by federal grants.
3.	$243,728, excluding those reimbursed by federal grants.
4.	$5,454,463, including both civil defence and other preparations for civilian measures in wartime, in so far as these are segregated in accounts. In some cases work is done for these purposes but paid for out of appropriations for the general purposes of the department concerned and is not separated in accounts.
5.	The government has already been using the term "emergency measures" to cover both civil defence and peacetime disasters, as well as preparations for the continuity of government in wartime.
6.	No.
7.	The government is preparing for publication material regarding protection against radioactive fall-out for people living in apartments. In addition, surveys are being conducted this year to investigate the protection afforded by existing larger buildings in urban areas and means of improving it.
8.	It is not considered in the public interest to publish detailed information relating to all the various sites from which elements of the government would operate outside of Ottawa in wartime.
9 and 10. Various responsibilities for wartime operations have been allocated by the government and by individual ministers, as reported to parliament from time to time. Other responsibilities may be expected to be assigned from time to time in future. The ministers responsible for these various departments and agencies in peacetime, and their deputies, designate the personnel who will be trained for wartime duties and who will take them on, if they can, should war occur. It may be necessary that various individuals be designated as alternatives, or in rotation if, as is now expected, special precautions become necessary because of the very short warning time that may be counted upon when missiles become the main threat to Ottawa. The lists of those being instructed to assume various duties in the event of war are still being compiled and revised. It is considered that publication of the names of these individuals would serve no useful purpose at the present time.
It should be added that those assigned to emergency duties will not be assured of safety, as the emergency facilities cannot provide protection against a nearby nuclear detonation. Protection against fall-out is being provided to enable work to be carried on in these locations. Persons assigned to emergency war duties will not be free to look after the safety of their families, as others will be doing, and will have to make other arrangements in respect of their dependents.

Monday, May 15, 1961
